units.title: I believe in God
units.eq: What does it mean to believe?

lessons.title: The Creed: a summary of our faith
lessons.idea: The Creed is the Church’s short summary of the faith, handed down from the apostles. “Creed” comes from the Latin credo, “I believe.” We pray the Nicene Creed at Sunday Mass and the Apostles’ Creed at Baptism and in the Rosary.
lessons.question: Why do we say the Creed together?
lessons.activity: “Creed in order” (25 min). Write the twelve articles of the Apostles’ Creed on strips. In teams, put them in order and sort them into three groups: Father, Son, Holy Spirit. Then read the Creed aloud together and mark each place where it is about God and where it is about us.
teach: The Creed is a summary of the faith (CCC 187). The Apostles’ Creed is the old baptismal creed of Rome; the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed comes from the councils of 325 and 381 (CCC 193–195).
It has three parts, for the three Persons of the Trinity: Father and creation, Son and redemption, Holy Spirit and the Church and eternal life (CCC 190).
Romans 10:9–10 links believing in the heart with confessing with the lips. “I believe” is personal, while at Mass we say “We believe” because faith is shared (CCC 167).
Do not reduce the Creed to memorizing. Ask at each article, “What does this change about how I live?”
talk: What do we believe about God the Father?
Why do we say “I believe” at Baptism and “We believe” in some places?
Which line of the Creed do you find easiest? Hardest?
quiz: “Creed” comes from the Latin for…|I hope|I pray|I sing|I believe|3|Credo.
The Creed is said at…|The mall|Mass|School|Soccer|1|CCC 188.
The Apostles’ Creed is mainly used at…|Baptism and the Rosary|Funerals only|Never|Weddings only|0|CCC 194.
lessons.life: Say the Apostles’ Creed slowly every night this week and notice one line each time.
lessons.saint: Basil the Great: a bishop who defended the faith and fed the hungry.
misc: “The Creed is just a prayer to recite.”
“Each person makes up their own creed.”
lessons.mem: “I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.” (Apostles’ Creed, first article)
lessons.hook: Ask a child to explain their favorite sport in one sentence. Then ask, “How would you sum up the whole Catholic faith in one minute?” The early Christians faced the same problem and the Creed was their answer.
lessons.assess: Ask children to say the first three articles from memory and to name the three Persons the Creed is organized around.

script.open: Put on a team jersey or hold a flag. Ask, “What does this say about you? When you wear a team’s jersey, everyone knows what you believe in. Christians have a ‘jersey’ too, a short statement of what we believe. It is called the Creed.”
teach: Say: “The word Creed comes from the Latin word credo, which means ‘I believe.’ The Creed is a short summary of what the Church believes, handed down from the apostles. St. Paul wrote, ‘If you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.’ (Romans 10:9) In 1 Corinthians 15:3-5, he gives an early summary: ‘Christ died for our sins… he was buried… he was raised on the third day.’”

Say: “We use two Creeds. The Apostles’ Creed is the oldest, from the early baptismal questions of Rome. At Baptism, the priest asks, ‘Do you believe in God, the Father almighty?’ and we answer ‘I do.’ We pray it in the Rosary. The Nicene Creed was written by bishops at the Council of Nicaea in 325, and completed at the Council of Constantinople in 381. We say it on Sundays at Mass. These councils had to state clearly what the Church believes, because some were teaching that Jesus was not truly God.”

Say: “The Apostles’ Creed has twelve statements, called articles. They are about God the Father and creation; Jesus; the Holy Spirit and the Church. When we say ‘I believe,’ we don’t only mean ‘I think this is true.’ We mean: ‘I trust God and give my life to him.’ We say ‘I believe’ at Baptism and at Mass. It is the way we say yes to God.”
ask: What does ‘Creed’ mean? (I believe.)
When do we say the Nicene Creed? (At Mass on Sundays and holy days.)
Why does the Church have a Creed? (To state clearly what we believe, handed down from the apostles.)
practice: Write the twelve articles of the Apostles’ Creed on strips of paper (one per strip).
Divide into teams. Each team gets a mixed-up set and races to put them in order.
Check against the text. For each article, a team member says, in plain words, what it means.
Pray the Creed together slowly.
script.close: Pray the Apostles’ Creed together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray the Creed with your family, and listen for it at Mass.”

tryit: Put the twelve statements of the Apostles’ Creed in order.
Say what each one means.
Say the Creed together.
lessons.saintStory:
Basil was born around the year 330 in Cappadocia, in what is now Turkey, to a family of saints: his grandmother, his parents, his sister Macrina and his brothers Gregory and Peter are all remembered as saints. He studied in Athens, where he became close friends with another future saint, Gregory of Nazianzus.
Basil gave up a promising career to become a monk, and wrote rules to help monks live together. In 370 he became bishop of Caesarea. During a terrible famine he sold his own goods and gave out food himself. He built a large complex of buildings for the sick and poor, a hospital, that people called the Basiliad.
Basil also defended the faith when many people denied that the Son and the Holy Spirit are truly God. He died in 379. Two years later, the Council of Constantinople finished the Creed we say at Mass on Sundays, using the ideas Basil had defended.

lessons.title: Faith: a gift and a choice
lessons.idea: Faith is both God’s gift and our free answer. It means trusting God and believing everything he has revealed because he cannot deceive or be deceived. Abraham and Mary show what faith looks like.
lessons.question: Who is an example of faith in the Bible?
lessons.activity: “Heroes of faith” (25 min). In groups, read Hebrews 11:1–3 and then one story: Abraham (Genesis 12:1–4), Noah (Genesis 6–7), Mary (Luke 1:38). Each group makes a one-minute newscast: “What did they trust God to do? What did it cost?”
teach: Faith is a gift of God and a human act (CCC 153–155). We choose to believe, but we could not without grace.
Faith is certain because God is truth (CCC 156–157). It is reasonable, and it seeks understanding (CCC 158–159). Faith and science do not contradict.
Abraham is “the father of all believers” (CCC 144–146) and Mary is the model of faith (CCC 148–149). Hebrews 11 lists many more.
Faith must be lived and grow. We nourish it with Scripture, the sacraments and prayer, and it can be lost if neglected (CCC 162).
talk: What do you trust God for?
Who has taught you to believe?
quiz: Faith is…|A rule|Only knowledge|Only a feeling|A gift and a free response|3|CCC 153-155.
A model of faith is…|Abraham|Herod|Pilate|Judas|0|Hebrews 11:8.
Faith needs…|Trust and understanding|Luck|Silence|Wealth|0|CCC 158.
lessons.life: Tell a family member one thing you believe about God and why.
lessons.saint: Mary: the model of faith from Nazareth to the cross.
misc: “Faith means believing without any reason.”
“If I have doubts, my faith is gone.”
lessons.mem: “Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.” (Hebrews 11:1)
lessons.hook: Do a trust fall in pairs, or ask: “Would you step onto a bridge if someone you trusted said it was safe?” Faith in God is like that, but God is infinitely more trustworthy.
lessons.assess: Ask: “Is faith a gift or a choice? Give one example from Abraham or Mary.”

script.open: Hold up a pair of glasses and say, “If I take these off, I can’t see clearly. Faith is like a pair of glasses that helps us see what we cannot see with our eyes. Let’s find out what it is.”
teach: Read Hebrews 11:1-3: “Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.” Say: “Faith means trusting God and believing everything he has revealed, because God cannot deceive or be deceived. We can’t see God, but we believe because he has told us. It is like trusting a friend who always tells the truth.”

Say: “Faith is a gift and a choice. It is a gift because we can’t make ourselves have faith. It is God’s grace, given at Baptism, with the help of the Holy Spirit. But it is also a choice: God does not force us. We respond freely: ‘Yes, I believe.’ And faith is not against reason. God made our minds, and he gave us reasons to believe. But faith goes further than what we can prove.”

Say: “Hebrews 11 lists heroes of faith. Abraham left home not knowing where he was going. Noah built an ark when there was no rain. Moses led the people through the sea. Mary said yes to the angel. Faith is not just believing facts, but acting on them. It is trusting enough to act. And faith grows when we use it, like a muscle. We pray, ‘Lord, increase my faith.’”
ask: What is faith? (Trusting God and believing what he has revealed.)
Why can we trust God? (He cannot lie or be wrong.)
Who are examples of faith? (Abraham, Noah, Moses, Mary.)
practice: Split into groups. Each group reads Hebrews 11:1-3 and then one story: Abraham (Genesis 12:1-4), Noah (Genesis 6:13-22), Moses (Exodus 14) or Mary (Luke 1:26-38).
On a poster, they draw the person and write: What did God ask? What did they do? What did it cost? What happened?
Post the posters, and do a gallery walk.
Each child writes one sentence on what they learn about faith.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.” (Mark 9:24) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell someone about a time you had to trust God.”

tryit: Read Hebrews 11 and one story of faith.
Make a poster of your hero of faith.
Say what it cost them to trust God.
lessons.saintStory:
Mary was a young girl from Nazareth, probably in her teens, when the angel Gabriel greeted her as “full of grace.” He told her she would conceive and bear a son, the Son of the Most High. She did not understand everything, and she asked, “How can this be?” But she said, “Let it be done to me according to your word.”
Her faith was tested again and again. She gave birth in a stable. She fled to Egypt. She lost Jesus for three days in Jerusalem and did not understand his answer. She watched her Son be rejected and crucified. And she stood at the foot of the cross. The Gospels say that she “kept all these things in her heart.”
Elizabeth said to her, “Blessed is she who believed.” Mary shows us what faith is: trusting God even when we don’t see the whole picture.

lessons.title: One God in three Persons
lessons.idea: There is one God in three Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The three are distinct, equal and not three gods. The Trinity is the central mystery of our faith and shows that God is love.
lessons.question: Why is the Trinity a mystery?
lessons.activity: “Good and bad pictures” (25 min). Show common analogies (the shamrock, water as ice/liquid/steam, the sun with light and heat). For each, children decide: What does it help show? Where does it fail (modalism, partialism)? Then draw the Trinity’s true image: a circle of love, giving and receiving. Read Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:13.
teach: The Trinity is “the central mystery of Christian faith and life” (CCC 234). We know it only because God revealed it in Jesus (CCC 237).
God is one in being (substance) and three in Persons (CCC 253–254). The Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Spirit, yet each is fully God.
John says “God is love” (1 John 4:8). Love needs someone to love, and in the Trinity God is a communion of love from all eternity (CCC 221).
Every analogy limps. St Patrick’s shamrock helps with “three in one” but can suggest God has parts. Say it is a mystery we can know but never exhaust.
talk: How does the Sign of the Cross proclaim the Trinity?
Why is God a family of love?
quiz: The Trinity is…|One Person|A symbol|Three gods|One God, three Persons|3|CCC 253.
The Persons are…|Mere roles|Equal|Unequal|Ranked|1|CCC 253-255.
A mystery is…|A lie|A truth we can’t exhaust|A secret|A riddle|1|CCC 237.
lessons.life: Pray the Glory Be slowly three times this week, thinking of each Person.
lessons.saint: Gregory of Nazianzus: a bishop called “the Theologian” because he spoke so well about the Trinity.
misc: “God is one Person who plays three roles.”
“The Father is greater than the Son and Spirit.”
lessons.mem: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” (Sign of the Cross; Matthew 28:19)
lessons.hook: Trace the Sign of the Cross slowly. Ask, “Who do we name?” Then ask, “Is that three gods?” Take answers, then say: today we find out why the answer is no.
lessons.assess: Ask children to explain, in their own words, why the Trinity is not three gods, and to name what each Person is traditionally said to do (create, redeem, sanctify).

script.open: Hold up three candles. Light them one at a time. Ask, “Is this one fire or three?” Let children think. Then hold them together. “The flames are three, but the light is one. It’s not a perfect picture, but it gets us started.”
teach: Read Matthew 28:19. Say: “Jesus told the apostles to baptize ‘in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’ Notice: it’s one ‘name,’ but three Persons. Paul ended a letter with a blessing: ‘The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.’ (2 Corinthians 13:13) The Trinity is the central mystery of the faith.”

Say: “There is one God in three Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The three Persons are distinct, which means they are not the same person. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit. But they are also equal: each is fully God, with the same power and love. And there are not three gods, but one God. This is a mystery: a truth so great that we cannot fully understand it, but we can know it is true because God has revealed it.”

Say: “Every picture of the Trinity is incomplete. A shamrock suggests three leaves, but three leaves of one plant are parts, and each Person is fully God. Water that is ice, liquid and steam, but one substance at a time, not all at once. The sun with its light and heat, but those are less than the sun. These pictures can help a little, and each fails somewhere. The truth of the Trinity shows us that God is love: a relationship of giving and receiving love, within God himself. And God invites us into it.”
ask: How many Gods are there? How many Persons? (One God, three Persons.)
Why does the shamrock picture not work perfectly? (The leaves are parts; each Person is fully God.)
What does the Trinity show about God? (God is love, a communion of Persons.)
practice: Show three or four common pictures of the Trinity (shamrock, water in three states, sun and heat and light, an egg).
In pairs, children decide for each: what does it help us see, and where does it fail?
Share ideas in the whole group.
Then try making a better picture or just a ‘statement’ of the faith in words: “The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, and they are one God.”
script.close: Pray the Glory Be, slowly, together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Explain the Trinity to someone, using the Sign of the Cross.”

tryit: Look at the pictures that try to show the Trinity.
Decide which are good and which mislead.
Make a better one.
lessons.saintStory:
Gregory was born around the year 329 in Cappadocia, and he studied in Athens with his friend Basil. He wanted to live a quiet life of prayer and writing, but his father, who was a bishop, and the Church needed him. In 380 the Christians in Constantinople asked him to come and lead them, in a city where many people had stopped believing that Jesus is truly God.
He preached powerful sermons in a small church, which he called the Anastasia, “the Resurrection.” In five famous talks, he explained the Trinity: that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three Persons, but one God. He said that the Father is the source, the Son is begotten, and the Spirit proceeds.
The Church calls him “the Theologian.” At the Council of Constantinople in 381, he helped to set the words of the Creed we pray today. Gregory shows us that the Trinity is not a puzzle to solve, but a mystery to love.

lessons.title: God made everything good
lessons.idea: God created everything out of nothing, freely and out of love. Creation is good, ordered and meant to praise him. Faith and science answer different questions: science how, faith who and why.
lessons.question: What does Genesis teach about creation?
lessons.activity: “Seven days, one message” (30 min). Make a seven-column poster for Genesis 1. Under each day, children write what God made and draw it. Under it add the repeated refrain “And God saw that it was good.” Discuss: what is the author teaching? (God is the source, creation is good, humans are special). Compare it with Psalm 104.
teach: God created the world freely, “out of nothing,” by his word (CCC 296–298). Creation is not an accident or a part of God.
Genesis 1 teaches who made the world and why, not a science textbook (CCC 337–349). The Church sees no conflict between faith and genuine science (CCC 159, 283–284).
Everything is “very good” (Genesis 1:31) and shows God’s wisdom (CCC 299, 339). Creation is a gift and we are stewards of it (CCC 2415–2418).
Respond to questions about evolution simply: the Church allows that God may have used natural processes, but teaches that each human soul is directly created by God (CCC 366).
talk: What does Genesis 1 teach about creation?
How can we care for it?
quiz: God created…|From a dream|Out of nothing|From a rock|From another god|1|CCC 296.
Creation is…|Evil|Accidental|An illusion|Good|3|CCC 299.
Humans are…|Equal to animals only|Gods|An accident|The summit of creation|3|CCC 343.
lessons.life: Choose one way to care for creation (recycle, plant) and do it daily.
lessons.saint: Albert the Great: a scholar who studied nature and loved God.
misc: “Catholics must reject science.”
“Creation was made from God’s own substance.”
lessons.mem: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.” (Genesis 1:1)
lessons.hook: Hold up a painting and ask, “Who made this? Can I see the artist?” Then look at a leaf or a photo of space. “What can this tell us about its maker?”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What does ‘out of nothing’ mean? Name two things Genesis 1 teaches about creation.”

script.open: Bring something natural: a leaf, a shell, a stone, a feather. Pass it around. Say, “Look at this carefully. Who made it? How was it made? Those are two different questions, and today we will see why both are good.”
teach: Read Genesis 1:1-5 and part of Psalm 104. Say: “‘In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.’ God created everything out of nothing. Not from something else, not because he needed to, but freely and out of love. Everything God made is good. Over and over Genesis says, ‘And God saw that it was good.’ Then, when he made people, ‘it was very good.’”

Say: “Creation has an order. Genesis 1 shows days: light, sky and sea, land and plants, sun and moon, fish and birds, animals and people, and rest. Each step prepares for the next. It teaches us that God is a God of order, and that he made everything for a purpose: to praise him and to serve us. God blessed the world, and then he rested on the seventh day, a holy day.”

Say: “Science and faith ask different questions. Science asks how things work, and when. It studies the universe with experiments. Faith asks who made it, and why. Faith says that God is behind it all. Genesis is not a science textbook. It uses images and a story to teach that God made everything, that it is good, and that we are made in his image. The Church teaches that there is no real conflict between faith and science, because the same God is the author of both truth and creation.”
ask: What does it mean that God created ‘out of nothing’? (He didn’t need anything to make it.)
What is the difference between how science and faith answer questions? (Science: how; faith: who and why.)
Why is creation good? (God made it, and he is good.)
practice: Give each child a long sheet divided into seven columns.
Under each day, children draw what God made, and write one thing it shows about God: his power, his love, his order, his creativity, his care.
On the seventh day, draw how we rest and worship.
Pair up and share your favorite day.
script.close: Pray Psalm 104:24: “O Lord, how manifold are your works!” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Go outside, find something God made, and thank him.”

tryit: Make a seven-day poster for Genesis 1.
Write what each day shows about God.
Say thank you for each.
lessons.saintStory:
Albert was born around the year 1200 in Germany. He joined the Dominicans and became a great teacher in Paris and Cologne. His most famous student was Thomas Aquinas, whom he met in Paris. Thomas was quiet and everyone called him the Dumb Ox, but Albert said that his bellowing would fill the world.
Albert was fascinated by nature. He studied plants, animals, rocks, stars and the weather, and wrote books about them. He did experiments and went out to observe things for himself. He believed that studying creation was a way to know the Creator. He knew that faith and reason do not conflict, because God is the author of both.
He was called “the Universal Doctor” because he knew so much. Albert is the patron saint of scientists. He shows that studying God’s world can be a way to praise him.

lessons.title: Angels and humans
lessons.idea: God made angels, pure spirits who serve and praise him, and humans, who are body and soul in the image of God. Each person has a guardian angel and a soul that never dies.
lessons.question: What are the differences between angels and people?
lessons.activity: “Angels and us” Venn (25 min). A Venn diagram labelled Angels, Humans and Both. Children place cards: has a body, has a soul, has intellect, has will, serves God, was made in his image, can die, never dies. Discuss. Then pray the Guardian Angel prayer.
teach: Angels are spiritual, personal, immortal creatures with intellect and will (CCC 328–330). Scripture shows them as messengers (Luke 1:26–38) and protectors (Psalm 91:11; Matthew 18:10).
The three archangels named in Scripture are Michael, Gabriel and Raphael (feast September 29). Each person has a guardian angel (CCC 336).
Humans are body and soul united as one person (CCC 362–365) and made in God’s image (CCC 355–357). The soul is immortal and directly created by God (CCC 366).
Some angels freely rebelled and became demons (CCC 391–395). Teach this briefly and without fear: Jesus has already won.
talk: How can you thank your guardian angel?
quiz: Angels are…|Spirits|People who died|Statues|Stars|0|CCC 328.
People are…|Angels|Bodies only|Spirits only|Body and soul|3|CCC 362.
Gabriel announced…|To Moses|To David|To Mary|To Noah|2|Luke 1.
lessons.life: Pray to your guardian angel each morning.
lessons.saint: Raphael the Archangel: an angel who guided a young traveler and healed.
misc: “People become angels when they die.”
“Angels are cute babies with wings.”
lessons.mem: Angel of God, my guardian dear, to whom God’s love commits me here, ever this day be at my side, to light and guard, to rule and guide. Amen.
lessons.hook: Ask, “What is invisible but real?” (air, love, a song). Say that angels are real beings we cannot see, and that you are a mix: a body you can see and a soul you cannot.
lessons.assess: Ask children to name two ways angels and humans are alike and two ways they differ.

script.open: Turn off the lights and say, “Close your eyes. Imagine a bright being with great power, who has no body. What would you think?” Let children share. “Angels are real. Let’s see what the Bible says.”
teach: Say: “Angels are pure spirits. They do not have bodies, as we do. God made them before the world and they serve him. They have minds and wills, they are very powerful, and they are always praising God. The word ‘angel’ means ‘messenger,’ which describes what they do for us. Psalm 148:2: ‘Praise him, all his angels.’ Three are named in the Bible: Michael, Gabriel and Raphael.”

Say: “Angels are also our helpers. Every person has a guardian angel from the moment of birth, as Jesus teaches in Matthew 18:10. Angels protect us and guide us. They bring our prayers to God. But we should not worship angels. We worship only God, and we thank him for sending them.”

Read Genesis 2:7: “Then the Lord God formed man of dust from the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.” Say: “Humans are different. We are a union of body and soul. Our body is made of matter, and our soul is a spiritual part that God creates for each person. The soul never dies. We are made in God’s image, and called to know and love him. Angels are pure spirit. Animals have bodies and life but not an immortal soul. Humans are in the middle, matter and spirit together, which is why we are special.”
ask: What are angels? (Pure spirits who serve and praise God.)
What is a guardian angel? (An angel God gives each person to protect and guide.)
How are humans different from angels and from animals? (Body and soul; made in God’s image.)
practice: Draw a large Venn diagram with three areas: Angels, Humans, Both.
Give out cards with traits: has a body, has a soul, is a pure spirit, praises God, can know and love, has a guardian angel, can sin, is made by God, will die, will rise.
Children place each card in the right area and say why.
Finish by saying the Guardian Angel prayer together.
script.close: Pray the Guardian Angel prayer together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank your guardian angel every night.”

tryit: Sort the cards: angels, humans, both.
Place them on the Venn diagram.
Say what makes humans special.
lessons.saintStory:
The Book of Tobit tells of a young man named Tobias who had to make a long journey. His father, Tobit, was old and blind. Tobias needed a guide, and a stranger offered to go with him. His name was Azariah, but he was really the archangel Raphael, which means “God heals.”
On the journey, Tobias was attacked by a big fish, and Raphael told him to take the fish’s heart, liver and gall, which would be used as medicine. Raphael led him safely to a distant city, helped him find a good wife named Sarah, who was in great trouble, and brought him home. There, he told Tobias to put the gall on his father’s eyes, and Tobit could see again.
When the journey was over, Raphael told them who he was: “I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand before the Lord.” He tells us to thank God and praise him. Raphael shows how angels help us on the road.

lessons.title: The fall and God’s promise
lessons.idea: Adam and Eve freely disobeyed God, and sin and death entered the world. Their sin wounded human nature, and we are born needing redemption. But God immediately promised a Savior.
lessons.question: What does “original sin” mean?
lessons.activity: “The fall in four scenes” (25 min). Read Genesis 3 in four parts: the temptation, the sin, the hiding, the promise (3:15). For each, children draw and name what changed (trust, shame, blame, hope). Underline the first word of hope in Genesis 3:15 (“enmity… he will strike your head”). Trace it to Jesus and Mary.
teach: Original sin: Adam and Eve freely disobeyed and lost original holiness (CCC 397–400). We inherit a fallen human nature, not their personal guilt (CCC 404–405).
The effects: ignorance, suffering, death and an inclination to sin (concupiscence) (CCC 405–409). Baptism removes original sin but the inclination remains.
Genesis 3:15 is the “protoevangelium,” the first announcement of the Gospel: a descendant of the woman will defeat the serpent (CCC 410–411). Christ is the new Adam, Mary the new Eve (CCC 411).
Be honest and calm: the story explains why the world has evil without blaming God. It ends in hope.
quiz: Original sin is…|A story|Mere imagination|A rule|The first sin that wounded human nature|3|CCC 404.
Baptism…|Doesn’t help|Is optional|Adds sin|Frees us from original sin|3|CCC 1263.
God promised…|A boat|Nothing|A Redeemer|Punishment only|2|Genesis 3:15.
lessons.life: Make a short thank-you prayer for Baptism.
lessons.saint: Irenaeus: a bishop who showed that Mary undid what Eve did.
misc: “Eve’s sin was eating an apple.”
“Babies are born guilty of Adam’s personal sin.”
lessons.mem: “I will put enmity between you and the woman… he shall bruise your head.” (Genesis 3:15)
lessons.hook: Show a nice, clean white cloth and spill a little water or ink on it. “What happens when something spoils?” Say sin spoiled God’s good creation, and ask who could fix it.
lessons.assess: Ask: “What did the first sin break? What did God promise right away?”

script.open: Show a beautiful vase and ask a child to hold it. Say, “If I dropped it, what would happen? Something beautiful would break. Today we hear about something even more precious that was broken, and how God planned to fix it.”
teach: Say: “God made Adam and Eve good, and he put them in a garden with everything they needed. They were close to him. He gave them one rule: do not eat the fruit of one tree. A serpent, the devil, tempted Eve, ‘Did God really say that?’ He told her, ‘You will not die. You will be like God.’ They disobeyed. This is the Fall, also called original sin.”

Say: “They lost the gift of friendship with God and the gifts that went with it. They felt shame and hid. Their relationship with each other was broken: Adam blamed Eve. They were sent out of the garden, and death entered the world. Original sin wounded human nature. Because of this first sin, all of us are born with a weakened nature, inclined to sin, and without the life of grace. We are not guilty of Adam’s personal sin, but we inherit its effects. That is why we need to be saved, and why we are baptized.”

Say: “But God did not give up! Genesis 3:15 is the first announcement of good news. God said to the serpent, ‘I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he shall bruise your head.’ It is called the ‘protoevangelium,’ the first gospel. A descendant of the woman will defeat the serpent. We know that is Jesus, with Mary beside him. The story of the Fall is sad, but it ends with a promise.”
ask: What was the first sin? (Adam and Eve disobeyed God.)
What are the results of original sin? (A wounded nature, suffering, death, the tendency to sin.)
What did God promise right away? (A Savior who would defeat the serpent.)
practice: Read Genesis 3 in four parts: the temptation, the sin, the hiding, the promise.
After each part, children draw a quick picture on a four-panel sheet, and write a word for what changed: trust, shame, blame, hope.
Underline the promise in Genesis 3:15 together, and trace it to Jesus and Mary.
Share a word or phrase from their panels.
script.close: Pray: “Thank you, God, for the promise of a Savior.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family: sin is real, but God’s promise is stronger.”

tryit: Tell the story of the fall in four scenes.
Draw what changed in each.
Find the first promise of hope.
lessons.saintStory:
Irenaeus was born around the year 130 in Smyrna, and as a boy he had listened to Polycarp, the old bishop who had known the apostle John. He moved to Gaul (France) and became a priest in the city of Lyon. After the bishop was killed in a persecution, in 177, he was chosen to take his place.
Some teachers were saying false things: that the world was evil, and that Jesus only seemed to be human. Irenaeus wrote a big book, Against Heresies, to answer them. He taught that God made the world good, that Jesus truly became man, and that he came to heal everything that was damaged by sin.
He wrote about Adam and Eve and about Mary, seeing that Eve’s “no” was undone by Mary’s “yes.” He is the one who wrote, “The glory of God is man fully alive.” Irenaeus helps us see the story of the fall, and of God’s promise.

lessons.title: Conceived by the Holy Spirit
lessons.idea: “Conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.” The Son of God took a human nature in Mary’s womb. This is the Incarnation, the greatest event in history.
lessons.question: What does “incarnation” mean?
lessons.activity: “Annunciation in action” (25 min). Act the scene, then freeze-frame it. Each child steps in as Mary and says what she is thinking. Then compare Matthew’s account (Joseph, Matthew 1:18–25) with Luke’s (Mary). Fill a two-column chart: “What Matthew tells,” “What Luke tells.”
teach: The Incarnation: the Son of God took flesh (CCC 461–463) to save us, show us God’s love, be our model and make us partakers of the divine nature (CCC 457–460).
The virginal conception shows that Jesus is God’s Son and the new creation is God’s work (CCC 496–498). Mary remained a virgin before, during and after the birth (CCC 499–507).
Mary’s “yes” (Luke 1:38) is the model of faith and freedom (CCC 494). Jesus is one Person with two natures, divine and human (CCC 464–469).
Distinguish the Immaculate Conception (Mary’s conception) from the virginal conception (Jesus’). This confuses many adults too.
talk: Why does it matter that Jesus is both God and man?
quiz: Jesus was conceived by…|An angel|The Holy Spirit|Joseph|A prophet|1|CCC 484.
The Incarnation means…|God became man|A symbol|A myth|Man became God|0|CCC 461.
Mary is…|A queen only|A prophet only|A goddess|A virgin|3|CCC 496.
lessons.life: Pray the Angelus or a Hail Mary at noon.
lessons.saint: Anselm: a bishop who asked, “Why did God become man?”
misc: “Immaculate Conception means Jesus’ conception.”
“Jesus became God at his baptism.”
lessons.mem: “Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” (Luke 1:38)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 1:26–38 dramatically with three readers. Stop at “How can this be?” Ask, “What would you have said?” then finish with Mary’s answer.
lessons.assess: Ask: “Who is the Father of Jesus’ human life? Who is his mother? Why does this matter?”

script.open: Show a large paper with the word “yes” written on it. Say, “Can one word change history? There was a time when one young woman said one word, and it changed everything.”
teach: Read Luke 1:26-38 aloud. Say: “In the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a town in Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin named Mary, who was engaged to Joseph. He said, ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.’ Mary was troubled, and the angel said, ‘Do not be afraid. You will conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High.’ Mary asked, ‘How can this be, since I have no husband?’ The angel said, ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you.’ Mary said, ‘Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.’”

Say: “This is the Incarnation: the Son of God took a human nature in Mary’s womb. We say in the Creed, ‘He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.’ Jesus has no human father. His conception is a miracle, the work of the Holy Spirit. Mary stayed a virgin. This is the greatest event in history. The Son of God, who had no beginning, became a human being, while still being God. Mary’s ‘yes’ was free, and it made it possible.”

Say: “Why does it matter? Because it shows how much God loves us. He came into our world as one of us, to teach, to heal, and to save. ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.’ (John 1:14) We celebrate the Annunciation on March 25, nine months before Christmas, and we pray the Angelus every day at morning, noon and evening to remember it.”
ask: What is the Incarnation? (God’s Son took a human nature in Mary’s womb.)
Who is Jesus’ father? (God the Father; Jesus has no earthly father by nature; Joseph was his foster father.)
What did Mary say to the angel? (Let it be done to me according to your word.)
practice: Choose volunteers to be Gabriel, Mary and narrators. Act out Luke 1:26-38 slowly, with simple movements.
Freeze the scene at Mary’s answer. Tap the shoulder of other children one at a time to step into Mary’s place and say aloud what she might have been thinking.
Discuss how it felt to say yes.
Pray the Angelus together, or the Hail Mary.
script.close: Pray the Angelus or the Hail Mary. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray the Angelus at noon with someone.”

tryit: Act out the Annunciation.
Freeze the scene.
Step in as Mary and say what she felt.
lessons.saintStory:
Anselm was born in 1033 in northern Italy, and as a young man he left home to study and became a monk at a monastery in Normandy. He loved to think about God. He became abbot and, later, Archbishop of Canterbury in England.
His motto was “faith seeking understanding.” He did not want to prove God to make himself believe. He wanted to understand better what he already loved. He wrote a book called “Why God Became Man” (Cur Deus Homo), in which he explained that only someone who is both God and man could repair the damage done by sin.
Anselm quarreled with two English kings who tried to control the Church, and he was sent into exile twice, but he never gave up. He shows how the Incarnation is the greatest event in history, and worth thinking about deeply.

lessons.title: Suffered, died, rose
lessons.idea: “Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried; on the third day he rose.” Jesus freely gave his life to forgive our sins, and the Resurrection shows that death and sin are defeated.
lessons.question: Why did Jesus have to suffer?
lessons.activity: “Holy Week map” (30 min). Make a timeline Palm Sunday to Easter Sunday. For each day add one event and one sign we see in church today. Draw the three “days” of the Triduum. Use Luke 24 to tell the Easter morning story. Plan a Holy Week prayer calendar.
teach: Jesus died “for our sins” according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3; CCC 599–605). He was not a victim of fate but gave his life freely (CCC 609–614). The responsibility belongs to all sinners, not to any one people (CCC 597–598).
The Resurrection is both historical and transcendent: the tomb was empty and he appeared to many, in a glorified body (CCC 639–646). It is the foundation of our faith (CCC 651, 1 Corinthians 15:14).
He “descended to the dead” to free the righteous who waited (CCC 632–635). The Cross is also a sacrifice, renewed in the Mass (CCC 1366).
Take care with the Passion narratives, which have been misused to blame the Jews. The Church firmly rejects this (CCC 597).
talk: What did Jesus say on the cross?
What does it mean that he rose?
quiz: Jesus died…|By accident|For nothing|For our sins|By chance|2|CCC 601.
The Resurrection took place on…|Never|The third day|The tenth day|The first day|1|CCC 638.
All sinners…|Are responsible for Christ’s death|Only Pilate|Only soldiers|None|0|CCC 598.
lessons.life: Pray the Stations of the Cross on a Friday in Lent.
lessons.saint: Simon of Cyrene: a stranger who carried Jesus’ cross.
misc: “The Jews killed Jesus.”
“The Resurrection is only a symbol.”
lessons.mem: “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures… he was raised on the third day.” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4)
lessons.hook: Read part of John 19:16–30 with the lights low. Pause on “It is finished.” Ask, “Was that defeat or victory?” Then go quiet.
lessons.assess: Ask children to tell the events from Holy Thursday to Easter in order and say what each reveals about God’s love.

script.open: Say, “Imagine a week. On Sunday, people shout and cheer. By Friday, a few of the same people are shouting something else. What could happen in one week to change a city?” Let children guess. “This is the story of Holy Week.”
teach: Tell the days: “Palm Sunday: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, and people shout ‘Hosanna!’ and lay down palm branches. Holy Thursday: At the Last Supper, he gives us the Eucharist and washes the feet of his disciples. Then he prays in the Garden of Gethsemane, and Judas hands him over. Good Friday: Jesus is tried, condemned by Pilate, scourged, crowned with thorns and made to carry the cross. He is crucified at Golgotha.”

Say: “Read John 19:30. ‘It is finished.’ Jesus gave his life freely to forgive our sins. He died, and was buried. The Creed says: ‘Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried.’ The Romans were responsible for killing Jesus, but all of us sinners are the reason he died. Jesus did it because he loves us. ‘Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.’”

Say: “Then, on the third day, Easter Sunday, Jesus rose. ‘He is not here, for he has risen.’ (Luke 24:6) The Resurrection is the foundation of our faith. It shows that Jesus is God, that sin and death are defeated, and that we will rise. Jesus did not just come back to his old life. He rose with a glorified body, never to die again. He appeared to Mary Magdalene, Peter, the disciples, and over five hundred people. Easter is the greatest feast of the Church year.”
ask: Why did Jesus die? (To forgive our sins, because he loves us.)
What does the Resurrection show? (Jesus is God, and death and sin are defeated.)
What is different about Jesus’ risen body? (It is glorified and will never die.)
practice: Give each child a long strip of paper, folded into seven or eight parts: Palm Sunday, Holy Thursday, Good Friday, Holy Saturday, Easter Sunday.
For each day, write one event and draw one sign (a palm branch, bread and cup, a cross, a tomb, a lamp).
Add a small note about where Simon of Cyrene appears.
Tell the week to a partner using the strip.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, you died and rose for us. Thank you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Retell Holy Week with your family.”

tryit: Make a timeline from Palm Sunday to Easter.
Add one event and one sign each day.
Point out where Simon helped.
lessons.saintStory:
The Gospels mention Simon in a few lines. He was a man from Cyrene, in North Africa, who had come to Jerusalem, probably for the Passover. As he was coming in from the countryside, the Roman soldiers grabbed him and forced him to carry the cross of Jesus, who was too weak to carry it by himself after being scourged.
We do not know what Simon thought. He may have been angry at first, because it was not his choice. But he walked behind Jesus all the way to the place called Golgotha. Mark’s Gospel describes him as “the father of Alexander and Rufus,” which suggests that his sons were known to the first Christian readers, and that Simon’s family became Christians.
Simon shows us what Jesus said: “Whoever wishes to come after me must take up his cross and follow me.” Sometimes we help carry the cross without choosing it.

lessons.title: Ascended and will come again
lessons.idea: “He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father; he will come again to judge the living and the dead.” Jesus reigns now, is present in his Church, and will return in glory.
lessons.question: What will happen at the end of time?
lessons.activity: “Already and not yet” (25 min). Two columns: “Jesus has already…” (risen, ascended, sent the Spirit, given the Eucharist) and “Jesus will yet…” (return, judge, make all things new). Children fill with Scripture clues (Matthew 28:20; Acts 1:11; Matthew 25:31–46). Then write one thing to do while we wait.
teach: At the Ascension Jesus enters into glory and reigns at the Father’s right hand (CCC 659–664). He did not leave us: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).
He will come again to judge the living and the dead (CCC 678–679). The judgment concerns love: “I was hungry and you gave me food” (Matthew 25:31–46).
We do not know the day or hour (CCC 673–674). Our task is to be ready, to love and to spread the Gospel.
Avoid frightening children with end-times speculation. Stress hope: Jesus returns as King and Friend.
talk: What will happen when he returns?
quiz: Jesus ascended…|To Rome|Into heaven|To the desert|To Egypt|1|Acts 1:9.
He will return…|Never|Quietly|In glory|As a baby|2|CCC 671.
He will judge…|Only kings|The living and the dead|Only the dead|No one|1|CCC 678.
lessons.life: Write a note to Jesus telling him how you hope to welcome him.
lessons.saint: Bede the Venerable: a monk who worked until his last day.
misc: “Jesus left and is no longer with us.”
“We can predict the date of the end.”
lessons.mem: “Behold, I am with you always, to the close of the age.” (Matthew 28:20)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Where is Jesus right now?” Take answers (heaven, with us, in the Eucharist). Then read Acts 1:9–11 and ask why the disciples stared at the sky.
lessons.assess: Ask children to explain where Jesus is now, how he is present, and what he will do when he returns.

script.open: Hold a sign that says “Already” on one side and “Not yet” on the other. Ask, “If you plant a seed, the plant is ‘already’ there in a way, but ‘not yet’ grown. Today we talk about two things Jesus has done, and one he will do.”
teach: Read Acts 1:6-11. Say: “Forty days after Easter, Jesus appeared to his disciples for the last time. He told them to wait for the Holy Spirit and be his witnesses ‘to the end of the earth.’ Then, as they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. Two men in white said, ‘Why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus will come in the same way as you saw him go.’ This is the Ascension.”

Say: “The Creed says: ‘He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.’ The right hand of the Father is a way of saying that Jesus has the place of honor and power. Jesus is not far away. He reigns now as King and Lord. He is also close to us in his Church: in the sacraments, in the Bible, in each other, and in the poor. He prays for us. And he has prepared a place for us.”

Say: “The Creed goes on: ‘He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.’ This is the Second Coming. Nobody knows when. Jesus will come back at the end of time, to make everything right. We live ‘already’ in his kingdom, and we wait for it to be complete. So we pray, ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’ And we try to be ready. Jesus will judge everyone with perfect justice and mercy.”
ask: What does ‘seated at the right hand of the Father’ mean? (Jesus has the place of honor and power.)
Where is Jesus now? (In heaven, and also with us through his Church.)
What will Jesus do when he comes again? (Judge the living and the dead, and complete his kingdom.)
practice: Make a two-column chart: “Jesus has already…” and “Jesus will…”
In the first column: was born, taught, died, rose, ascended, sent the Holy Spirit, gave us the Church. In the second: come again in glory, judge, bring a new heaven and a new earth.
Add what we do while we wait: pray, serve, tell others.
Share and pray together “Come, Lord Jesus.”
script.close: Pray: “Come, Lord Jesus.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask your family what you can do to be ready for Jesus.”

tryit: List what Jesus has already done.
List what we are still waiting for.
Say: “Come, Lord Jesus.”
lessons.saintStory:
Bede was born around 673 in the north of England, and when he was seven his family sent him to the monastery of Wearmouth, and later to Jarrow. He lived there for the rest of his life. He loved to study, to teach and to write. He wrote on the Bible, on nature and time, and about the history of England, The Ecclesiastical History of the English People. He is sometimes called the “Father of English history.”
Bede was a gentle man who sang the psalms with his brothers every day. When he was dying, in 735, he was still working, dictating a translation of the Gospel of John into English to a young helper. The helper said, “There is only one sentence left.” Bede said, “Write it quickly.” When it was finished, he said, “It is finished,” and died, praying the Glory Be, around the feast of the Ascension.
He is the only English person named a Doctor of the Church. Bede shows us how to live looking toward Jesus’ return, working to the end, and trusting him.

units.title: The Holy Spirit and the Church
units.eq: Who is the Holy Spirit and what is the Church?

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit gives life
lessons.idea: The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Trinity, “the Lord, the giver of life.” He inspired the Scriptures, formed the Church and lives in us. Fire, wind, water, oil and the dove are signs of his work.
lessons.question: Where do we see the Spirit at work?
lessons.activity: “Symbols of the Spirit” trail (30 min). Stations: water (fill a bowl), oil (smell chrism-scented oil), fire (candle), wind (feathers), dove (picture of the baptism of Jesus), seal (stamp). At each, read a verse (John 3:5, 1 John 2:20, Acts 2:3, John 3:8, Mark 1:10, Ephesians 1:13) and write what the sign says about the Spirit.
teach: The Holy Spirit is God, equal to the Father and Son (CCC 243–248, 685). We pray, “I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son.”
He spoke through the prophets and inspired Scripture (CCC 687–688, 702–716). He was active at the Annunciation, the baptism of Jesus and Pentecost.
He is the “soul of the Church” and gives gifts and fruits (CCC 797–798, 1830–1832). Learn the seven gifts: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord.
The Spirit is a Person, not an energy. Use personal language: he teaches, comforts, guides.
talk: Where do you see the Spirit working?
quiz: The Holy Spirit is…|A force|A saint|The third Person of the Trinity|An angel|2|CCC 685.
Symbols of the Spirit include…|Dove, fire, wind|Cat, dog, cow|Stone, tree, star|Ring, key, crown|0|CCC 694-701.
The Spirit gives…|Money|Rules only|Gifts|Toys|2|Isaiah 11:2.
lessons.life: Learn the seven gifts of the Spirit.
lessons.saint: Catherine of Siena: a young woman filled with the Spirit who spoke boldly to popes.
misc: “The Holy Spirit is a force.”
“The Spirit only came at Pentecost.”
lessons.mem: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love.
lessons.hook: Fan a candle flame safely or blow a feather. “You cannot see wind but you can see what it does.” Ask where the Spirit has been at work in the stories they know.
lessons.assess: Ask children to name three symbols of the Holy Spirit and say what each shows.

script.open: Blow out a candle, or use a pinwheel with a fan. Ask, “What made the wind move? We can’t see it, but we see what it does. The Holy Spirit is like that. Today we will meet the Spirit.”
teach: Say: “The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Trinity. The Nicene Creed calls him ‘the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, who with the Father and the Son is adored and glorified.’ He is God, equal to the Father and the Son. We cannot see him, but he is at work. He inspired the prophets and the writers of Scripture. He overshadowed Mary. He came upon Jesus at his baptism. He came upon the apostles at Pentecost.”

Read John 16:13: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” Say: “Jesus promised to send the Holy Spirit to teach and guide us. The Spirit lives in the Church and in each baptized person. He gives us life, helps us pray, tells us what is true, gives us gifts and makes us holy. He also makes the Church one.”

Say: “The Bible uses symbols to show what the Spirit does. Water: he gives new life, as in Baptism. Oil: he anoints and strengthens us, as in Confirmation. Fire: he warms, cleanses and gives courage, as at Pentecost. Wind or breath: he is the breath of God’s life. A dove: peace, as at Jesus’ baptism. A cloud and light: God’s presence. Each tells us something about how the Spirit works.”
ask: Who is the Holy Spirit? (The third Person of the Trinity, God.)
What did the Spirit do at Pentecost? (Came to the apostles and the Church began.)
What are some symbols of the Spirit? (Water, oil, fire, wind, dove.)
practice: Set up five stations: water (a bowl to touch), oil (a scented oil to smell), fire (a candle, watched from a distance), wind (a fan or paper to blow), dove (a picture).
At each, children read a short Scripture verse and write what the symbol shows about the Spirit.
Rotate every four minutes.
Each child picks one symbol and draws it with a sentence.
script.close: Pray the “Come, Holy Spirit” prayer. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask the Holy Spirit for help every morning.”

tryit: Visit the Spirit’s symbols: water, oil, fire, wind, dove.
Say what each one shows.
Draw your favorite.
lessons.saintStory:
Catherine was born in 1347 in Siena, Italy, the twenty-third of twenty-five children. When she was about six, she had a vision of Jesus, and she decided to give her life to him. Her parents wanted her to marry, but she cut her hair and refused. She became a Dominican tertiary, which means she lived in the world, in her family home, with a rule of prayer.
Catherine spent her time in prayer and caring for the sick, especially people with plague. She couldn’t write at first, but she dictated hundreds of letters to leaders, even to kings and popes. At the time, the popes were living in Avignon, France, and Catherine wrote to Pope Gregory XI to return to Rome. In 1377 he did.
She died in Rome in 1380, at thirty-three. She is a Doctor of the Church. Catherine shows how the Holy Spirit gives courage and wisdom to ordinary people.

lessons.title: The Church as the Body of Christ
lessons.idea: The Church is the Body of Christ. Jesus is the head and we are members, each with different gifts. Everyone is needed, and what happens to one member affects all.
lessons.question: What is your part in the body?
lessons.activity: “Parish body” (25 min). Draw a large body. Children label parts with real parish roles: eyes (lectors), hands (volunteers, servers), voices (choir), feet (missionaries, visiting the sick), heart (those who pray), and add their own. Write one gift each child has to offer.
teach: Paul compares the Church to a body (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; CCC 787–791). Christ is the head, the Spirit the soul, and we are members joined by Baptism.
The Church is also the People of God and the Temple of the Spirit (CCC 781–786, 797). These images complement each other.
“If one member suffers, all suffer together” (1 Corinthians 12:26). The Body of Christ is nourished by the Eucharist (CCC 805–807).
Help children see that no gift is small: the smile of a greeter matters as much as a homily.
talk: Why do we need each other?
quiz: The head of the Body is…|The Pope|The president|Christ|The priest|2|CCC 792.
Each member…|Is needed|Is a spectator|Is optional|Doesn’t matter|0|1 Corinthians 12:22.
Baptism makes us…|Visitors|Spectators|Members of the Body|Customers|2|CCC 1267.
lessons.life: Offer to help at your parish in one concrete way.
lessons.saint: Katharine Drexel: a rich young woman who gave everything to serve others.
misc: “The Church is just the building.”
“I can follow Jesus without the Church.”
lessons.mem: “Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.” (1 Corinthians 12:27)
lessons.hook: Ask a volunteer to try to write while their hand is tied behind their back, or hop on one foot. “What happens when a part is missing?” Read 1 Corinthians 12:12.
lessons.assess: Ask each child to name a gift they have and how it serves the Body.

script.open: Show a picture of a human body, and ask, “If one part says to another, ‘I don’t need you,’ what would happen?” Let children share ideas. “St. Paul used this picture to describe the Church.”
teach: Read 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 in summary. Say: “Paul says: ‘Just as the body is one and has many members, so it is with Christ.’ The Church is the Body of Christ. Jesus is the head, and we are the members, the parts. Each part has a different job. The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I don’t need you.’ If one part suffers, all suffer. If one is honored, all rejoice.”

Say: “This means that everyone in the Church is needed. Not just the priest or the Pope. Some are teachers, some are singers, some are helpers, some pray, some work with the poor. Each has gifts from the Holy Spirit, and each gift is for the good of all. We are baptized into one body, and we belong to each other.”

Say: “Jesus is the head, so he gives the body life and direction. The Holy Spirit is the soul of the body, who gives life to all members. When we receive Communion, we become more united with Jesus and with one another. When one of us sins, it harms the whole body. And when we do good, it strengthens everyone.”
ask: Who is the head of the Church? (Jesus.)
What does it mean that we are members of one body? (We all belong and we all need each other.)
What gift do you bring to the body? (Take answers.)
practice: Draw a large human body on a poster.

Label the parts with real roles in your parish: eyes (lectors who see and read God’s word), mouth (cantors and preachers), hands (those who serve and help), feet (those who visit the sick, missionaries), ears (listeners), heart (those who pray).
Write names of real people next to each role, and add yourself.
Discuss: what happens if one part is missing?
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, help us work together as one body.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank someone in our parish for their part.”

tryit: Draw a big body.
Label each part with a person in your parish.
Say how each one is needed.
lessons.saintStory:
Katharine Drexel was born in 1858 in Philadelphia, into one of the richest families in the United States. Her father was a banker. She grew up with servants and travel, but her parents also gave to the poor, and her stepmother opened their home to the needy twice a week.
When she traveled out west, she saw the poverty of Native Americans and African Americans, who had few schools. When she met the Pope and asked him to send missionaries, he suggested, “Why don’t you become a missionary yourself?” She did. She gave away her inheritance and, at thirty-three, founded the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament.
Katharine’s sisters opened dozens of schools and missions across the country, including Xavier University in New Orleans, the first Catholic university for African Americans. She lived to be ninety-six. She shows that everyone in the Body of Christ has a part to play.

lessons.title: Marks of the Church
lessons.idea: The Creed says the Church is one, holy, catholic and apostolic. These four marks come from Christ and the Spirit, and they help us recognize the Church he founded on Peter and the apostles.
lessons.question: Which mark do you notice most?
lessons.activity: “Four marks scavenger hunt” (30 min). Around the parish or in photos, find examples: one (the same Mass in every language), holy (a saint’s statue, the tabernacle), catholic (flags of countries in the parish), apostolic (the bishop’s photo, the list of popes). Record and share.
teach: One: one Lord, one faith, one Baptism (Ephesians 4:4–6; CCC 813–822). Unity does not mean uniformity: many rites and cultures. Wounds to unity exist, and we pray for Christian unity (CCC 817–822).
Holy: because Christ and the Spirit make her holy, though her members are sinners (CCC 823–829). Catholic: whole and for all (CCC 830–856).

Apostolic: founded on the apostles, with their teaching handed on through bishops in succession from them (CCC 857–865). Christ said, “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18).
Teach respectfully about other Christians: the Church recognizes much truth and holiness among them (CCC 817–819).
talk: How is she holy even with sinners?
quiz: The Church is one because of…|One building|One country|One Lord, one faith, one Baptism|One language|2|Ephesians 4:5.
The Church is catholic because…|She is Roman|She has the fullness of faith for all people|She is old|She is big|1|CCC 830.
Apostolic succession is…|Teachers|Priests wearing robes|Bishops following the apostles|Popes only|2|CCC 861.
lessons.life: Find your bishop on the diocesan site and pray for him.
lessons.saint: Peter Canisius: a teacher who explained the Church’s faith to many people.
misc: “If the Church is holy, no Catholic can sin.”
“Catholic just means a Roman church.”
lessons.mem: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.” (Matthew 16:18)
lessons.hook: Ask, “If you lost your phone, how would you know yours from a lookalike?” Introduce marks as the signs by which we recognize Christ’s Church.
lessons.assess: Ask children to give each mark and one real sign of it.

script.open: Show a picture of a church building, and a picture of a different building. Ask, “How can you tell which is a church? What are the signs?” Take answers. “How can you tell which Church is the one Jesus founded? It, too, has signs, called marks.”
teach: Say: “We say in the Creed: ‘I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.’ These are the four marks of the Church. They come from Christ and the Holy Spirit, and they help us recognize the Church Jesus founded. In Matthew 16:18, Jesus said to Peter, ‘You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.’”

Say: “One: the Church is one because she has one Lord, one faith, one Baptism, and one leader after Peter, the Pope. In Ephesians 4:4-6, Paul says, ‘one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism.’ Holy: the Church is holy because Christ, her head, is holy, and gives her the sacraments, the Gospel and the Holy Spirit. Her members sin, but she is holy in what she gives us. Catholic means ‘universal.’ The Church is for all people and all times. She has the fullness of faith and the means of salvation. Apostolic: she is built on the apostles and still taught by their successors, the bishops, in an unbroken line from them.”

Say: “These marks are not just signs for others. They are also a call for us. We should work for unity, strive for holiness, share the faith with everyone, and stay faithful to what the apostles taught. When the Church sees her members fail, she turns to Christ to be renewed. And the marks remind us that Jesus’ promise holds: the gates of hell will not prevail.”
ask: Name the four marks. (One, holy, catholic, apostolic.)
What does ‘catholic’ mean? (Universal.)
What does ‘apostolic’ mean? (Built on the apostles; led by their successors.)
practice: Go around the parish, or look at photographs, to find examples of each mark: one (the same Mass in every church; a picture of the Pope), holy (the sacraments, saints’ statues), catholic (people of different nationalities, a world map), apostolic (the bishop’s name in the Mass, a list of Popes).
Take notes or photos in teams.
Each team presents what it found.
Add a sentence: how can I live this mark?
script.close: Pray the line from the Creed: “I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look for the four marks this week.”

tryit: Go on a scavenger hunt for the four marks.
Find examples of one, holy, catholic and apostolic.
Write or photograph what you find.
lessons.saintStory:
Peter Canisius was born in 1521 in the Netherlands. He studied in Cologne and became a Jesuit. He lived at a time of confusion, when many Catholics in Germany were leaving the Church, and many were uncertain what the Church taught.
Peter traveled on foot or by horseback across Germany, Austria, Bohemia and Switzerland, preaching, teaching and starting schools. He wrote catechisms: books to explain the faith in simple questions and answers. His small catechism was used for hundreds of years, and he wrote for different ages.
He is called “the second apostle of Germany.” He died in 1597. Peter Canisius shows that the Church’s marks of unity, holiness, universality and apostolic roots are real, and that teaching them is a loving work.

units.title: Communion of saints and life everlasting

lessons.title: Communion of saints
lessons.idea: The communion of saints unites all who belong to Christ: the Church on earth, the souls being purified, and the saints in heaven. We share holy things and pray for one another.
lessons.question: How do you ask the saints to pray?
lessons.activity: “Make a litany” (25 min). Each child chooses a saint and writes one invocation (e.g., “St Francis, teach us to love creation”). Combine the lines into a class litany. Pray it together. Read Hebrews 12:1–2.
teach: “Communion of saints” means both holy persons and holy things, above all the Eucharist (CCC 946–948). All members share spiritual goods.
Three states of the Church: pilgrims, souls being purified, the blessed in heaven (CCC 954). The saints intercede for us (CCC 956–957).
We honor saints; we worship God alone. Their lives are models and their prayers help (CCC 2683).
Link to praying for the dead on All Souls (November 2) and visiting cemeteries (CCC 958).
talk: Whom do you ask to pray for you?
quiz: The communion of saints joins…|Only heaven|Heaven, earth and purgatory|Only the dead|Only the living|1|CCC 954.
Saints pray…|Only for angels|Against us|For us|Never|2|CCC 956.
A litany is…|A game|A prayer of invocations|A song only|A speech|1|CCC 2678.
lessons.life: Say a litany with your family.
lessons.saint: Dominic: he promised to help his friends from heaven.
misc: “Praying to saints is worshiping them.”
“Saints are far away and don’t care.”
lessons.mem: “We are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses.” (Hebrews 12:1)
lessons.hook: Show a family tree with some names in gold. Ask, “Who are the people who are looking out for you?” Add the saints to the list.
lessons.assess: Ask children to explain the difference between honoring saints and worshiping God.

script.open: Show a photo of a family with grandparents who have passed away, or a family tree. Ask, “Are they still part of the family, even though they’re not here? The Church is a family that includes those who’ve died.”
teach: Say: “The Apostles’ Creed says, ‘I believe in the communion of saints.’ It means all those who belong to Christ are connected in one big family. There are three groups: the Church on earth, the pilgrim Church, still on the journey. The Church in purgatory, the souls who have died in God’s friendship and are being made ready for heaven. And the Church in heaven, the saints, who see God face to face. Death does not break the bonds of love.”

Read Hebrews 12:1-2: “Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses… let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus.” Say: “The saints are like a stadium full of people cheering us on. They pray for us, and we can ask them to pray for us, just as we ask friends. They are not rivals to Jesus. They bring us to him.”

Say: “The communion of saints also means that we share holy things: the sacraments, the prayers and the merits of Christ. We can pray for the souls in purgatory, especially at Mass. We pray for the whole Church. And we honor the saints by imitating their lives. A litany is a prayer that lists the saints one at a time, with the response, ‘pray for us.’”
ask: What are the three parts of the communion of saints? (Church on earth, in purgatory, in heaven.)
How do the saints help us? (They pray for us and show us how to live.)
How can we help the souls in purgatory? (Pray for them, offer Mass.)
practice: Each child chooses a saint they like.
On a card, they write a line for a class litany: “St. ___, teach us to ___.” For example: “St. Francis, teach us to love creation.”
Gather in a circle. One child reads each line, and everyone responds, “Pray for us.”
Add the Guardian Angel prayer.
script.close: Pray the litany you wrote together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for a family member who has died.”

tryit: Write a line for a litany of saints.
Choose a saint and what they teach us.
Pray it together.
lessons.saintStory:
Dominic de Guzmán was born in Spain around 1170. He became a priest and, as he traveled, he saw that many people did not know the faith, so he began a new order, the Order of Preachers, now called the Dominicans, to teach and preach. He gathered a group of friars who would study, pray and travel on foot.
Dominic was a joyful, gentle man, who loved to pray at night. He taught people to pray the Rosary, according to tradition. By the time he was fifty-one, his friars had spread across Europe. He became ill on a trip to Bologna, in Italy, and his friars gathered round him. He told them, “Do not weep; I shall be more useful to you after my death, and I shall help you then more effectively than during my life.”
He died on August 6, 1221. Dominic’s promise is what the communion of saints means: those in heaven help those on earth.

lessons.title: Forgiveness of sins
lessons.idea: “I believe in the forgiveness of sins.” Jesus gave the apostles the power to forgive sins. We receive forgiveness at Baptism, and again in the Sacrament of Reconciliation when we confess, are sorry, and receive absolution.
lessons.question: Why does the Church forgive sins?
lessons.activity: “Steps of Confession” (25 min). Arrange cards: examine conscience, be sorry, confess, receive penance, absolution, do the penance. Role-play with a puppet priest or an adult. Practice the Act of Contrition. Read John 20:21–23.
teach: On Easter evening Jesus breathed on the apostles and said, “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven” (John 20:21–23; CCC 976–983). The Church continues this through bishops and priests.
The sacrament has acts of the penitent: contrition, confession, satisfaction, and the priest’s absolution (CCC 1450–1460, 1480). The priest is bound by the seal of confession (CCC 1467).
Mortal sin breaks our friendship with God; venial sin weakens it (CCC 1854–1864). The sacrament restores grace and peace.
Reassure children: Confession is meeting a merciful Father. Prepare them to go without fear.
talk: Why did Jesus give this power?
How do you feel after forgiveness?
quiz: Sins are forgiven in…|Mass only|School|Prayer only|Baptism and Reconciliation|3|CCC 977-979.
Jesus gave this power to…|The apostles|Kings|Nobody|Angels|0|John 20:23.
The priest forgives…|Never|In Christ’s name|By himself|By magic|1|CCC 1461.
lessons.life: Make an examination of conscience at bedtime.
lessons.saint: Alphonsus Liguori: a gentle confessor and the patron of confessors.
misc: “Priests forgive sins on their own power.”
“I only have to confess if I feel guilty.”
lessons.mem: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.” (John 20:23)
lessons.hook: Tell a story of a child who broke a window and hid. How did they feel? What relieved them? “God does not want us to carry sin; he wants to lift it.”
lessons.assess: Ask a child to walk through the steps of Confession in order and explain what each means.

script.open: Put a puddle of muddy water on a sheet, and a bucket of clean water. Ask, “Is this clean? How do we get the mud out?” Say, “When we sin, our soul gets muddy. God gave us a way to clean it.”
teach: Say: “In the Creed we say, ‘I believe in the forgiveness of sins.’ God forgives our sins in two main ways. At Baptism, original sin and all personal sins are washed away. But after Baptism, we can sin again. So Jesus gave us another sacrament: Reconciliation, also called Confession or Penance. On Easter night, Jesus breathed on the apostles and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven.’ (John 20:21-23) The apostles passed this power on to bishops and priests.”

Say: “There are five steps: One: Examine your conscience: think about your sins, with the Ten Commandments or a guide. Two: Be sorry for your sins. This is called contrition. Three: Confess your sins to the priest, honestly and completely. Four: Receive a penance from the priest: a prayer or good act to repair the harm and begin again. Five: Receive absolution, when the priest says, ‘I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’ Then we promise to try not to sin again, and we give thanks.”

Say: “The priest can never reveal anything that is said in Confession. This is called the seal of Confession. Sometimes we feel afraid or embarrassed. But the priest is there in the person of Christ, to forgive, to guide and to help. Many people feel lighter and happier afterward. God never tires of forgiving us.”
ask: Who gave the apostles power to forgive sins? (Jesus.)
What are the steps of Confession? (Examine, be sorry, confess, penance, absolution.)
What is the seal of Confession? (The priest can never tell what he hears.)
practice: Write the five steps on cards: examine your conscience, be sorry, confess, receive penance, absolution.
Mix them up. In teams, put them in order, and say what happens at each.
Practice the Act of Contrition aloud, line by line.
Quietly think about one thing you want to be sorry for (without telling anyone).
script.close: Pray the Act of Contrition together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Plan a time for Confession with your family.”

tryit: Put the steps of Confession in order.
Say what happens in each.
Practice the Act of Contrition.
lessons.saintStory:
Alphonsus was born near Naples, Italy, in 1696. He was very smart and became a lawyer at sixteen. But in 1723 he lost an important case, because he had missed a key paper, and he was so ashamed that he gave up law and decided to become a priest.
He worked among the poor, in the slums of Naples, and in the countryside, where he found that most people were uneducated about faith and had no one to teach them. He founded a congregation, the Redemptorists, to preach to the poor. He also wrote books, including a guide for confessors that helped them be kind and wise, and not harsh. He wanted people to feel welcome.
Alphonsus became a bishop and lived to ninety-one. He is the patron of confessors. He shows that Confession is a gift of God’s mercy, and priests should offer it with gentleness.

lessons.title: Resurrection of the body and life everlasting
lessons.idea: “I believe in the resurrection of the body and life everlasting.” Our bodies will rise at the end, transformed like Christ’s. Those who love God will live with him forever in heaven.
lessons.question: What does the Creed promise?
lessons.activity: “What will heaven be like?” (25 min). Read Revelation 21:1–5 and 1 Corinthians 15. List what Scripture says (no tears, no death, God dwells with us, new heaven and earth). Children sketch it and write a prayer for someone who has died.
teach: At death the soul is separated from the body and judged (CCC 1021–1022). At the end of time the body will rise and be reunited with the soul (CCC 988–1004). Christ’s Resurrection is the pattern (CCC 999).
Heaven is seeing God face to face and sharing his joy (CCC 1023–1029). Purgatory purifies those who die in friendship with God (CCC 1030–1032). Hell is real: free refusal of God (CCC 1033–1037).
The “new heaven and new earth” means creation is renewed, not destroyed (CCC 1042–1050).
Handle the topic of death with warmth. Some children will have lost loved ones.
talk: What will our bodies be like?
quiz: At the end, bodies will…|Vanish|Stay dead|Rise|Become spirits|2|CCC 988.
Heaven is…|Perfect communion with God|A cloud|A nap|A game|0|CCC 1024.
We prepare by…|Luck|Fame|Love and faith|Money|2|CCC 1021.
lessons.life: Pray for someone who has died, using “Eternal rest.”
lessons.saint: Lazarus: the friend of Jesus whom he raised from the dead.
misc: “We become angels when we die.”
“Our bodies are just thrown away at death.”
lessons.mem: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard… what God has prepared for those who love him.” (1 Corinthians 2:9)
lessons.hook: Show a seed and a flower. Read 1 Corinthians 15:36–44. “What you sow is not the body that shall be.” Ask what might be different about a risen body.
lessons.assess: Ask: “What happens to our bodies at the end? What is heaven?”

script.open: Say, “Close your eyes. Think about a person or pet you loved who has died. It is okay to feel sad. Jesus felt sad too. Today we learn what he promised us.”
teach: Say: “The last words of the Creed are: ‘I believe in the resurrection of the body and life everlasting.’ This means that when we die, our soul goes to God to be judged. But at the end of time, Christ will come, and our bodies will be raised and joined again to our souls. We will rise, as Jesus did. Paul explains this in 1 Corinthians 15: ‘For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.’ Our new bodies will be transformed: glorious, strong, not subject to death.”

Say: “What is heaven like? Scripture uses images: a wedding feast, a city of gold, a garden, light, a home. Revelation 21:4 says: ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more.’ But the main point is that we will be with God, and see him face to face. It is perfect happiness, with no sadness, sin or fear. We will see Mary, the angels, the saints and those we love.”

Say: “Not everyone chooses God. Hell is the state of those who refuse God’s love to the end. God does not send anyone to hell; people choose it by refusing him. Purgatory is the cleansing of those who die in God’s friendship but need purification before heaven. All who die in God’s grace are sure of heaven. Our choices matter, and we live in hope and trust in God’s mercy.”
ask: What do we believe will happen at the end? (Our bodies will rise and join our souls.)
What is heaven? (Life with God forever, seeing him face to face.)
What do we hope for? (To be with God, with all those we love.)
practice: Read Revelation 21:1-5 and 1 Corinthians 15:20-26 aloud.
Make two lists: “What the Bible tells us about heaven” (no more tears, God with us, new creation, no death, a home) and “What we still don’t know.”
Talk about how it feels to hope.
Draw or write a short description of what you look forward to most.
script.close: Pray: “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for someone who has died.”

tryit: List what Scripture says about heaven.
Sort it into: what we know and what we do not know.
Describe what you hope for.
lessons.saintStory:
Lazarus lived in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, with his sisters Martha and Mary. Jesus often stayed with them, and the Gospel says that Jesus loved them. When Lazarus became sick, his sisters sent word to Jesus, but by the time he arrived, Lazarus had been dead for four days.
Martha went out to meet Jesus and said, “If you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Jesus told her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.” When Jesus saw Mary and the others crying, he wept. Then he went to the tomb, and said, “Lazarus, come out!” And the man who had died walked out, still wrapped in burial cloths.
Tradition says that Lazarus later went to the island of Cyprus and became a bishop. Lazarus’ story points to what will happen to us, and it shows that Jesus is stronger than death.

lessons.title: Immaculate Conception
lessons.idea: By a special grace from God, Mary was conceived without original sin. The angel greeted her as “full of grace.” We celebrate the Immaculate Conception on December 8.
lessons.question: Why did God prepare Mary this way?
lessons.activity: “Full of grace” (20 min). Read Luke 1:28 in several translations. Discuss why “Hail, full of grace” is almost a name. Then write a card to Mary for December 8. Learn the Hail Mary’s first half.
teach: The dogma (Pius IX, 1854): from the first moment of her conception Mary was preserved from original sin, by the merits of Christ (CCC 490–493). Mary was saved by Christ in the most perfect way, in advance.
Luke 1:28 “kecharitomene,” “full of grace,” points to this fullness (CCC 490–491). Mary is the new Eve whose “yes” undoes Eve’s “no” (CCC 494).
