The feast is December 8 and is a holy day of obligation in the U.S. (CCC 1172). Our Lady of Lourdes said, “I am the Immaculate Conception” (1858).
Remember to separate this from Jesus’ virginal conception, a very common confusion.
talk: How can we imitate her purity?
quiz: The Immaculate Conception is about…|Joseph|The Church|Jesus’s birth|Mary’s conception|3|CCC 490.
It was defined in…|1054|2054|1954|1854|3|Ineffabilis Deus.
It celebrates on…|August 15|December 8|January 1|December 25|1|Liturgy.
lessons.life: Pray a Hail Mary on December 8.
lessons.saint: John Duns Scotus: a Franciscan who explained why Mary could be preserved from sin.
misc: “The Immaculate Conception means Jesus’ virgin birth.”
“Mary did not need a Savior.”
lessons.mem: Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee.
lessons.hook: Show a gift wrapped for a very special person. “If God were to prepare a mother for his Son, what would he do?” Let the children suggest, then connect to Gabriel’s greeting.
lessons.assess: Ask: “What does ‘Immaculate Conception’ mean? Whom does it honor, and why?”

script.open: Put out a spotless white cloth. Say, “Imagine God is going to be born on earth, and he needs a mother. Would he choose a mother with a spotless heart? What would he do to prepare her?”
teach: Read Luke 1:28 in a few translations: “Hail, full of grace” (Douay), “Greetings, favored one” (RSV), “Rejoice, highly favored one.” Say: “The angel doesn’t say ‘Mary.’ He calls her ‘full of grace,’ as if it were her name. The Greek word suggests that she has been filled with grace and remains so. The Church sees that she is completely filled with God’s favor.”

Say: “The Immaculate Conception is a special teaching. It means that from the first moment of her existence, Mary was kept free from original sin by a special gift from God, because she was to be the Mother of the Savior. ‘Immaculate’ means ‘without stain.’ It does not mean that Mary was conceived without a human father. It does not mean that she did not need a Savior. She was saved by Jesus’ death on the cross, in advance, in a special way. It is like being kept from falling into a pit, instead of being pulled out of one.”

Say: “Pope Pius IX declared this teaching in 1854. Four years later, at Lourdes, Mary told Bernadette, ‘I am the Immaculate Conception.’ We celebrate the feast on December 8. This shows us God’s great power to save, and the beauty of what he wants to do in each of us. Mary is the first and best example of what God’s grace can do.”
ask: What does ‘Immaculate’ mean? (Without stain.)
What did the angel call Mary? (Full of grace.)
Did Mary need a Savior? (Yes; she was saved by Jesus in advance.)
practice: Write Luke 1:28 from three Bible translations on the board, and read them.
Discuss why “full of grace” is almost a name, not just a greeting.
In pairs, write a sentence about why God would prepare Mary this way.
Pray the Hail Mary slowly, thinking about the words “full of grace.”
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray ‘O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us.’”

tryit: Read “full of grace” in different translations.
Say what the angel’s greeting shows.
Say the Hail Mary.
lessons.saintStory:
John Duns was born around 1266 in Scotland, in a place called Duns. He became a Franciscan friar and studied and taught at Oxford and Paris. He was so clever with arguments that he was called “the Subtle Doctor.”
He wrote about many things, but he is especially remembered for his answer to a hard question. People wondered how Mary could be free from original sin, since Jesus died to save everyone. Scotus said that Jesus could save Mary in an even greater way: by preventing her from being stained, in view of his coming death. As he wrote, “God could do it, it was fitting that he did, therefore he did it.”
Pope John Paul II declared him Blessed in 1993. Scotus helped the Church understand the Immaculate Conception.

lessons.title: Mother of God
lessons.idea: Mary is the Mother of God because the Son she bore is God. The Council of Ephesus (431) defined this title, “Theotokos,” to protect the truth about Jesus.
lessons.question: How does this protect the truth about Jesus?
lessons.activity: “Council in session” (30 min). Roleplay the Council of Ephesus: one side says Mary is only mother of Jesus’ humanity, the other that she is Mother of God. Children debate, then the “bishops” read Luke 1:43 (“the mother of my Lord”) and Galatians 4:4 and vote. Draw an icon of the Theotokos.
teach: Mary is the Mother of God, “Theotokos” (CCC 495, 509). The title does not say she is the origin of God but that her Son is God.
Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius, who separated Jesus into two persons (CCC 466). The title protects the Incarnation.
Elizabeth called her “the mother of my Lord” (Luke 1:43). Paul says God sent his Son “born of woman” (Galatians 4:4).
Mary’s motherhood extends to us (CCC 967–970). Many Eastern icons show her pointing to Jesus.
quiz: Mary is the Mother of…|God|The Spirit|The Trinity|The Father|0|CCC 495.
The Council of Ephesus was in…|1869|325|431|787|2|CCC 466.
Theotokos means…|God-bearer|Teacher|Queen|Saint|0|Tradition.
lessons.life: Look at an icon of the Theotokos and pray.
lessons.saint: Cyril of Alexandria: defender of the title.
misc: “Mary gave Jesus his divinity.”
“Calling Mary Mother of God makes her equal to God.”
lessons.mem: “And why is this granted me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43)
lessons.hook: Ask, “If you are the mother of a king, are you only the mother of the king’s body?” A mother is mother of the whole person. Mary is mother of the whole Jesus, who is God.
lessons.assess: Ask: “Why do we call Mary the Mother of God? What does this tell us about Jesus?”

script.open: Write two titles on the board: “Mother of Jesus’ human nature” and “Mother of God.” Ask, “Is there a difference?” Say, “In the year 431, the whole Church had to decide. We will have our own council.”
teach: Say: “Elizabeth said to Mary, ‘Why is this granted me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?’ (Luke 1:43) Paul said, ‘When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman.’ (Galatians 4:4) Mary is the mother of Jesus. And Jesus is God. So Mary is the Mother of God. This doesn’t mean she gave Jesus his divine nature, which always was. It means that the Person she bore is God.”

Say: “Think of your own mother. She is not just the mother of your body. She is the mother of you, a whole person. In the same way, Mary is the mother of the whole Person of Jesus, who is God the Son in human flesh. If you say she is only mother of his human nature, then you are splitting Jesus into two, and that is false.”

Say: “In 431, the Council of Ephesus defined this teaching, using the Greek title ‘Theotokos’: God-bearer. This protected the truth that Jesus is one Person, God and man. When we honor Mary as Mother of God, we are really honoring Jesus. And she is our mother too.”
ask: Why is Mary called Mother of God? (Because her Son, Jesus, is God.)
What does ‘Theotokos’ mean? (God-bearer.)
What does this title protect? (The truth that Jesus is God and man in one Person.)
practice: Set up a roleplay of the Council of Ephesus. Half the class are bishops who say Mary is only the mother of Jesus’ human nature, and half say she is the Mother of God.
Each side prepares arguments for ten minutes, using the readings.
Hold the debate, with a moderator. At the end, the “council” votes, and the teacher explains the Church’s decision.
Reflect: why did the title matter?
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary, especially: “Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Explain why Mary is the Mother of God.”

tryit: Act out the Council of Ephesus.
Argue both sides.
Say what is at stake.
lessons.saintStory:
Cyril was born in Egypt around 376, and became the patriarch of Alexandria in 412. He was a tireless defender of the faith. When Nestorius, the patriarch of Constantinople, taught that Mary should only be called Mother of Christ, but not Mother of God, Cyril wrote to him and then to the Pope in Rome.
The issue was bigger than a title. If Mary is not Mother of God, then Jesus is not truly God and man in one person. A council of bishops met in the city of Ephesus in 431. Cyril presided. They decided that Mary is rightly called Theotokos, “God-bearer,” and that Jesus is one Person, truly God and truly human. When the news reached the people of Ephesus, they celebrated in the streets with torches.
Cyril’s work protected the truth about Jesus. His story shows why Mary’s titles matter: they protect the truth about her Son.

lessons.title: Assumption and Queen of Heaven
lessons.idea: At the end of her earthly life Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory (the Assumption, August 15). She shares fully in her Son’s Resurrection and is Queen of Heaven. Her destiny shows what awaits us.
lessons.question: What does the Assumption show us?
lessons.activity: “Marian feasts calendar” (25 min). Create a year strip with Mary’s feasts: Jan 1 (Mother of God), Feb 11 (Lourdes), Mar 25 (Annunciation), May (month of Mary), Aug 15 (Assumption), Aug 22 (Queenship), Sept 8 (Birth), Oct 7 (Rosary), Dec 8 (Immaculate Conception), Dec 12 (Guadalupe). Pray the Salve Regina.
teach: Pius XII defined the Assumption in 1950: Mary, having completed her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory (CCC 966). It is the final fulfillment of her union with Christ.

The sign of the woman clothed with the sun in Revelation 12:1 is read by the Church as Mary and as the Church (CCC 972). The feast has been kept since the early centuries, and the Eastern Church calls it the Dormition.
Mary is Queen because her Son is King (CCC 966, 970). She is a mother who intercedes, not a rival to Christ.
August 15 is a holy day of obligation in the U.S. in most years. Check the calendar.
talk: Why is it a sign of hope?
How do East and West celebrate?
quiz: The Assumption is on…|January 6|November 1|December 25|August 15|3|Liturgy.
Mary was taken…|Spirit only|Soul only|Body only|Body and soul|3|CCC 966.
In the East this is called…|Dormition|Epiphany|Pascha|Lent|0|Tradition.
lessons.life: Pray a Rosary decade on a Marian feast.
lessons.saint: John of Damascus: a monk who preached about Mary’s falling asleep and being taken to heaven.
misc: “Mary is a goddess.”
“The Assumption is a late invention with no roots.”
lessons.mem: Hail, holy Queen, mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope.
lessons.hook: Ask, “If you could see a preview of the end of the movie, would you?” Mary’s Assumption is a preview of our own hope.
lessons.assess: Ask: “What happened to Mary at the end of her life? What does this show about us?”

script.open: Show a picture of the Assumption of Mary, and ask, “What is happening? Where is she going? What do you think this means?” Let children share. “This is one of the great feasts of the Church.”
teach: Say: “At the end of her life on earth, Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory. This is the Assumption, which we celebrate on August 15. The Church has believed this from the early centuries, and in 1950 Pope Pius XII declared it a dogma: a truth that must be believed. The Bible doesn’t describe it, but it shows Mary’s role in Jesus’ plan, and the book of Revelation, chapter 12, describes ‘a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.’”

Say: “Why do we believe it? Because Jesus is the Savior, and he would not let the body that carried him decay. Mary shared fully in his Resurrection. She is the first to share in what Jesus promised to all of us at the end of time: that our bodies will rise. The Assumption shows what awaits us. It gives us hope.”

Say: “Mary is also called Queen of Heaven. This is because her Son is the King of kings, in the line of David. In the royal family of Israel, the mother of the king was the queen mother, and she interceded for people. We honor Mary as queen, and we ask her to pray for us. We often pray the Hail, Holy Queen after the Rosary. Mary’s feasts give us a year of times to honor her.”
ask: What happened to Mary at the end of her life? (She was taken body and soul into heaven.)
Why do we believe in the Assumption? (She shared fully in Jesus’ Resurrection; the Church has always believed it.)
What does it show us? (What awaits us: the resurrection of the body.)
practice: Draw a strip with twelve months.

Mark Mary’s feasts: January 1 (Mary, Mother of God), February 11 (Our Lady of Lourdes), March 25 (Annunciation), May 31 (Visitation), August 15 (Assumption), September 8 (Birthday of Mary), October 7 (Our Lady of the Rosary), December 8 (Immaculate Conception), December 12 (Our Lady of Guadalupe).
Add a symbol for each.
Circle the Assumption and write a sentence.
script.close: Pray the Hail, Holy Queen, or the Hail Mary. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Celebrate Mary’s next feast with your family.”

tryit: Make a calendar of Mary’s feasts.
Add one fact for each.
Mark the Assumption.
lessons.saintStory:
John was born in Damascus, Syria, around the year 675, to a family of Christians who worked for the Muslim rulers. He was an official at the court, but he left his post and became a monk at the monastery of Mar Saba, near Jerusalem.
John wrote about the faith for the whole Church. His great book, The Fount of Knowledge, collected the teaching of the Fathers. He defended the use of holy images, saying that since God became visible in Jesus, we can honor sacred pictures. He also wrote beautiful hymns, and homilies on the falling asleep of Mary.
In his sermons, he says that Mary was taken to heaven, that her body did not see corruption, and she was made Queen. John shows how the Church from the early centuries believed in the Assumption.

units.title: The Sacraments (overview) and moral life
units.eq: How does God give us life and a path?

lessons.title: Seven sacraments
lessons.idea: The sacraments are seven effective signs, instituted by Christ and given to the Church, that give us his grace. Each has matter (the sign) and form (the words), and a minister.
lessons.question: What are the three groups of sacraments?
lessons.activity: “Seven sacraments matrix” (30 min). Build a chart with columns: sacrament, sign (matter), words (form), minister, grace. Children fill rows using cards. Check against the Catechism summaries. Highlight which are received once (Baptism, Confirmation, Orders).
teach: The sacraments are “efficacious signs of grace” (CCC 1131). They work “ex opere operato,” by Christ’s action, not by the minister’s holiness (CCC 1127–1128).
Grouped as initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist), healing (Reconciliation, Anointing), and service of communion (Holy Orders, Matrimony) (CCC 1210–1211).
Three leave a lasting mark (character): Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Orders (CCC 1121).
Receiving them with faith matters (CCC 1128). Grace is a gift, not magic.
quiz: There are…|Twelve|Five|Seven sacraments|Ten|2|CCC 1113.
Initiation sacraments are…|Anointing, Penance|Marriage, Orders|Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist|Mass, prayer|2|CCC 1212.
Sacraments give…|Cash|Luck|Grace|Fame|2|CCC 1131.
lessons.life: Say the names of the seven sacraments each night this week.
lessons.saint: John Chrysostom: the “golden-mouthed” preacher who taught about the sacraments.
misc: “Sacraments are only symbols.”
“A priest’s holiness makes the sacrament work.”
lessons.mem: The seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, Matrimony.
lessons.hook: Set out water, oil, bread, wine, a ring and a stole. Ask, “What do these do?” Hold up the idea that God uses ordinary things to give us his life.
lessons.assess: Ask children to name the seven, group them, and give the sign for three.

script.open: Give each child a coin. Say, “This is money. Does it have value? What gives it value? Because we agree on it. The sacraments are different. They have real power because Jesus gave them.”
teach: Say: “The sacraments are seven effective signs, instituted by Christ and given to the Church, through which we receive his grace. ‘Effective’ means they actually do what they signify. In Baptism, water washes. In the Eucharist, bread becomes Christ’s Body. In Mark 16:15-16, Jesus told his disciples, ‘Go into all the world… He who believes and is baptized will be saved.’ Jesus is the one at work in every sacrament; the priest acts in his person.”

Say: “Each sacrament has the same parts. Matter: the visible sign, such as water, oil, bread and wine. Form: the words that are said, such as ‘I baptize you…’ Minister: the person who celebrates it. And the recipient, the one who receives it with faith. When all these are present, Christ acts. The sacrament works because of what Christ does (ex opere operato), though the grace we receive depends on how open we are.”

Say: “The seven sacraments are in three groups. The sacraments of Christian initiation: Baptism, Confirmation and Eucharist. The sacraments of healing: Reconciliation and Anointing of the Sick. The sacraments at the service of communion: Holy Orders and Matrimony. They touch every stage of life: birth, growth, nourishment, healing, mission and love.”
ask: What is a sacrament? (An effective sign instituted by Christ that gives grace.)
What are the parts of a sacrament? (Matter, form, minister.)
Who is really acting in each sacrament? (Christ.)
practice: Draw a chart with the columns: Sacrament, Sign (matter), Words (form), Minister, What it gives.
Fill in each of the seven rows with the group, using the Catechism or a handout.
For example: Baptism, water, ‘I baptize you…’, priest or deacon (anyone in an emergency), new life.
Quiz each other on the chart.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, thank you for the sacraments.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Teach your family the seven sacraments.”

tryit: Fill in the seven sacraments chart.
Write the sign, the words and the minister.
Say what each gives.
lessons.saintStory:
John was born in Antioch around 347, and his mother, Anthusa, was widowed young and raised him in the faith. He studied to be a lawyer, but he became a monk and then a priest. He was such a gifted preacher that he was called “Chrysostom,” which means “golden mouth.”
In 398 he became the archbishop of Constantinople, the capital of the empire. He preached to rich and poor, and he spoke up against injustice, luxury and unkindness to the poor. He told the people that a poor person’s hungry belly is the altar of Christ, and that the Eucharist and care for the poor go together. Some powerful people did not like it, and he was sent into exile twice.
John died in 407, still on the way to a distant place of exile. He wrote beautiful homilies on Baptism and the Eucharist. He shows that the sacraments are for a life of love.

lessons.title: Virtues and conscience
lessons.idea: Virtues are good habits that help us do what is right. Conscience is the inner judgment that tells us what to do. We grow by practice, prayer and the sacraments.
lessons.question: Which habit would you like to grow?
lessons.activity: “Virtue habit tracker” (25 min). Each child picks one virtue (patience, honesty, generosity, courage) and designs a seven-day tracker with a daily action and a Friday reflection. Pair up and promise to check in.
teach: A virtue is “a habitual and firm disposition to do the good” (CCC 1803). Human virtues are acquired by practice; theological virtues (faith, hope, charity) are infused by God (CCC 1804–1813).
The four cardinal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance (CCC 1805–1809). Philippians 4:8 lists what to think about.
Conscience is a judgment of reason about the morality of an act. We must always follow it and also form it (CCC 1776–1785).
Vices are bad habits; the seven capital sins lead to others (CCC 1866). Name them without despair: virtue also grows.
quiz: A virtue is…|A feeling|A rule|A gift only|A good habit|3|CCC 1803.
Conscience is formed by…|Fear|Chance|The Church, Scripture, prayer|Peers|2|CCC 1785.
Practice builds…|Luck|Pride|Virtue|Fear|2|CCC 1804.
lessons.life: Choose a virtue and track it daily.
lessons.saint: Benedict: a monk who built a rule of daily habits for life.
misc: “Virtue is being naturally good.”
“Conscience can’t be wrong.”
lessons.mem: “Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure… think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8)
lessons.hook: Ask who has learned a skill by practice (piano, free throws). “Doing good is like that. Each good choice makes the next easier.”
lessons.assess: Ask each child to name a virtue, define it and tell how they will practice it.

script.open: Hold up a basketball (or a musical instrument). Ask, “How do you get good at basketball? Do you get good by watching, or by playing every day?” Say, “Being good at loving is the same.”
teach: Say: “A virtue is a good habit that helps us do what is right. A habit is something you do so often that it becomes easy. Brushing your teeth, or riding a bike. A good habit, like honesty, patience or generosity, makes it easier to choose well. Bad habits, called vices, do the opposite. Paul wrote, ‘Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely… think about these things.’ (Philippians 4:8)”

Say: “Conscience is the inner judgment that tells us whether an act is right or wrong. We grow in virtue by practice, repeating good acts. We need prayer and the sacraments, which give grace. We learn from the saints, from our parents, and from the Church’s teaching. Like Benedict’s Rule, a plan helps: set times to pray, work, study and rest.”

Say: “There are human virtues and divine ones. The four cardinal virtues are prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance. The three theological virtues are faith, hope and charity, which God gives us at Baptism. Other virtues, like patience, honesty and generosity, grow out of these. The more we practice, the more we become the person God made us to be.”
ask: What is a virtue? (A good habit that helps us do what is right.)
How do we grow in virtue? (Practice, prayer, sacraments, good examples.)
What is a vice? (A bad habit.)
practice: Each child chooses one virtue to work on: patience, honesty, generosity, courage, gratitude, kindness.
On a card, design a habit tracker: a grid of seven days, with a small action for each day (for example, honesty: tell the truth even when it is hard).
Add a space for a short prayer.
Share the plan with a partner, and agree to check in next week.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, help me grow in virtue.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Fill in your tracker each night.”

tryit: Pick one virtue.
Design a habit tracker for it.
Try it for a week.
lessons.saintStory:
Benedict was born around 480 in Nursia, Italy. His family sent him to Rome to study, but he saw so many people living badly that he left and went to live in a cave, in prayer. Other people heard about this holy young man and came to learn from him.
Benedict started twelve small monasteries, and then a larger one at Monte Cassino. For his monks he wrote a short rule of life, a plan for each day: time for prayer, time for work and time for reading. This is why monks are known by the motto “Pray and work.” The Rule is a plan for forming good habits and living together in peace. It starts with the word “Listen.”
He died around 547. Benedict’s Rule has shaped monasteries for 1,500 years. He shows how virtues are built by practice, one day at a time.

lessons.title: Beatitudes and Commandments
lessons.idea: The Ten Commandments and the Beatitudes work together: the commandments show the minimum of love, and the Beatitudes show the heights. Jesus sums up the law: love God and love your neighbor.
lessons.question: How are they connected?
lessons.activity: “Bridge” build (25 min). Draw a bridge between a commandment and a Beatitude (e.g., “You shall not kill” and “Blessed are the peacemakers”). Each pair makes two or three bridges and explains them. Read Matthew 22:37–40.
teach: The Decalogue was given to Moses after the Exodus, as a gift to a people already rescued (CCC 2056–2063). Jesus came not to abolish but to fulfill the Law (Matthew 5:17; CCC 577–582).
The two tablets: love of God (1–3) and love of neighbor (4–10) (CCC 2067–2068). Jesus says everything hangs on these two commands (Matthew 22:37–40; CCC 2055).
The Beatitudes are the vision of the happiness to which we are called (CCC 1716–1717). Together they teach: “Love and be happy.”
The commandments bind all people, always and everywhere (CCC 2072). They are written on our hearts.
talk: How do the Commandments relate to the Beatitudes?
What is Jesus’s summary of the law?
quiz: Jesus summarized the law as…|Fast|Pay taxes|Obey the king|Love God and love neighbor|3|Matthew 22:37-40.
The Beatitudes show…|The path to happiness|Wars|Taxes|The rules for the temple|0|CCC 1716.
The Commandments are…|Outdated|A burden|Arbitrary|A path of love|3|CCC 2062.
lessons.life: Pick a commandment and a beatitude to practice together.
lessons.saint: Paul Miki: a Jesuit who preached the Gospel from his cross and forgave his killers.
misc: “The Old Law no longer matters.”
“Beatitudes are suggestions; the commandments are rules.”
lessons.mem: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart… and your neighbor as yourself.” (Matthew 22:37–39)
lessons.hook: Show a fence along a mountain road and a view at the top. “The fence keeps us safe; the view is why we go.” The commandments keep us on the road; the Beatitudes show where it leads.
lessons.assess: Ask: “How do the commandments and Beatitudes fit together? Give one pair.”

script.open: Show a picture of a high-jump bar, or draw a line on the floor. Ask, “What is the minimum? What is the highest anyone can go?” Say, “The Ten Commandments are like the line you must not go below. The Beatitudes show how high we can go.”
teach: Read Matthew 22:37-40. Say: “A lawyer asked Jesus, ‘Which is the greatest commandment?’ Jesus said, ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment. And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.’ All Ten Commandments are about love.”

Say: “The Ten Commandments show us the minimum of love: do not kill, do not steal, do not lie. They protect people and our relationship with God. The Beatitudes show the heights of love: be merciful, make peace, be pure in heart, be poor in spirit. They go beyond what the law requires. Jesus said, ‘I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.’ The Beatitudes fulfill the commandments.”

Say: “For example, the commandment ‘You shall not kill’ tells us never to harm others. The Beatitude ‘Blessed are the peacemakers’ calls us to go beyond it: to actively make peace. The commandment ‘You shall not steal’ is fulfilled in ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit’: being generous and trusting God. They work together: the commandments are the foundation, and the Beatitudes are the roof.”
ask: What are the two great commandments? (Love God and love your neighbor.)
How are the commandments and the Beatitudes different? (Commandments: the minimum; Beatitudes: the heights of love.)
How do they fit together? (The Beatitudes fulfill the commandments.)
practice: Draw a bridge on paper. On one side write a commandment. On the other side write a Beatitude that goes with it.
Examples: “You shall not kill” and “Blessed are the peacemakers”; “You shall not steal” and “Blessed are the poor in spirit”; “You shall not lie” and “Blessed are the pure in heart.”
On the bridge, write one action that brings the two together.
Share your bridge, and choose one to practice.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, help us love as you love.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Choose a Beatitude to live this week.”

tryit: Build a bridge between a commandment and a Beatitude.
Say how they go together.
Choose one to practice.
lessons.saintStory:
Paul Miki was born in Japan around 1562, to a noble family. He studied with the Jesuits and became a Jesuit brother, an excellent preacher. In his time, Christianity had grown in Japan, but the ruler Hideyoshi feared it, and ordered Christians arrested.
In 1597, twenty-six Christians were arrested and marched about 600 miles through winter, to Nagasaki, to be executed on crosses. They were priests, brothers and lay people, including three boys, who were twelve to fourteen years old. Along the way they sang and prayed. Paul Miki, standing on his cross, preached to the crowd, saying that he was Japanese and a Christian, and that he forgave everyone who had ordered his death.
The martyrs of Japan show the meaning of the Beatitudes: blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, and blessed are the merciful. They lived what the commandments and the Beatitudes ask.

units.title: Prayer and Church year
units.eq: How do we live the faith each day?

lessons.title: Praying the Our Father
lessons.idea: The Our Father is the prayer Jesus gave us, “the summary of the whole Gospel” (Tertullian). It begins by calling God Father, then asks for seven things: God’s name, kingdom and will first, and then our bread, forgiveness, protection from temptation and deliverance from evil.
lessons.question: Which petition is most meaningful to you?
lessons.activity: “Seven petitions” paraphrase (30 min). Write each petition on a card and fold the group around it. Children rewrite it in their own words, draw an action that matches, and share. Read Matthew 6:9–13 and Luke 11:1–4. Pray it together very slowly.
teach: Jesus taught his disciples to pray when they asked (Luke 11:1; Matthew 6:9–13; CCC 2759–2761). Tertullian called it “the summary of the whole Gospel” (CCC 2761).
Calling God “Our Father” (“Abba”) shows adoption in Christ (CCC 2777–2785). “Our” means we pray with and for all (CCC 2786–2793).
The first three petitions are about God (hallowed name, coming kingdom, done will); the last four about us (bread, forgiveness, temptation, evil) (CCC 2803–2854).
Do not rush. The next lessons in later grades examine each petition in depth.
talk: Which petition do you pray most?
quiz: The Our Father has…|Three|Seven petitions|Five|Ten|1|CCC 2759.
The first petition is…|Deliver us|Give us bread|Hallowed be thy name|Forgive us|2|Matthew 6:9.
Jesus taught it to…|His disciples|Children only|Angels|Kings|0|Luke 11:1.
lessons.life: Pray the Our Father with a different intention each day.
lessons.saint: Teresa of Ávila: she wrote about the Our Father line by line.
misc: “God gives bad things to teach me lessons” (from “lead us not into temptation”).
“Daily bread just means food.”
lessons.mem: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
lessons.hook: Say the Our Father extremely fast, then ask what you said. Then slow down: “Jesus gave us each word on purpose.”
lessons.assess: Ask each child to say the Our Father and explain one petition in their own words.

script.open: Ask the class to say the Our Father together quickly. Then ask, “Did you think about the words? It’s easy to say a prayer fast, and miss what it says. Let’s unpack it.”
teach: Say: “The Church Father Tertullian called the Our Father ‘the summary of the whole Gospel.’ Jesus gave it to us in Matthew 6:9-13. It starts by naming God as ‘Our Father,’ which means we pray together, as a family. We say ‘Our’ because we pray with others. ‘Who art in heaven’ does not mean far away, but that God is above all.”

Say: “The first three petitions are about God. ‘Hallowed be thy name’: may your name be honored. ‘Thy kingdom come’: may your reign come on earth. ‘Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven’: may everyone do what you want. The next four are about us. ‘Give us this day our daily bread’: we ask for what we need, both bread and the Eucharist. ‘And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us’: we ask for forgiveness and promise to forgive. ‘And lead us not into temptation’: help us avoid temptation and to resist it. ‘But deliver us from evil’: protect us from the evil one, and from all evil.”

Say: “At Mass the priest adds, ‘Deliver us, Lord, from every evil.’ And we say, ‘For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours, now and forever.’ That is called the doxology. The Amen at the end means ‘so be it.’ Praying the Our Father slowly, thinking about the words, can be a lifelong prayer.”
ask: What are the first three petitions about? (God: his name, kingdom and will.)
What are the last four about? (Us: bread, forgiveness, help in temptation, protection from evil.)
What does ‘Our’ show? (We pray together as a family.)
practice: Give each child seven cards, one for each petition.

On the front, write the petition from the Our Father. On the back, write it in their own words and draw a picture. Example: “Give us this day our daily bread”: “God, please give me and my family what we need today.”
Fold them into a small booklet, or staple them.
Pray the Our Father together, using the booklets, slowly, one petition at a time.
script.close: Pray the Our Father very slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray your booklet with someone at home.”

tryit: Write each petition in your own words.
Fold the cards into a booklet.
Pray it slowly.
lessons.saintStory:
Teresa of Ávila was born in 1515 in Spain. When she was a teenager, she became a Carmelite nun. For about twenty years she found it hard to pray and was easily distracted. But then, after a deep experience in front of a statue of the suffering Christ, she changed. She began to pray with her whole heart.
Teresa started a reform of the Carmelites, with small convents of sisters who lived simply and prayed daily. In 1566 she wrote a book for her sisters called The Way of Perfection. A large part of it is about the Our Father: she goes through it line by line, explaining each petition. She wrote that when we say “Our Father,” we speak to the Father with Jesus, who is right beside us.
She is a Doctor of the Church. Teresa shows how a simple prayer can become a conversation with God that lasts a lifetime.

lessons.title: Forms and expressions of prayer
lessons.idea: There are five forms of prayer (blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise) and three expressions (vocal, meditation, contemplation). The psalms are the Church’s prayer book.
lessons.question: Which form of prayer helps you most?
lessons.activity: “Prayer menu” (25 min). Children build a menu of the five forms with a short example of each. Try a Lectio divina with Psalm 63:1–8: read, meditate, pray, rest. Journal a line afterward.
teach: The five forms (CCC 2626–2643): blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise. Each appears in the psalms.
The three expressions (CCC 2700–2724): vocal prayer uses words, meditation uses thought and imagination, contemplation is silent, loving attention to God.
The Psalms have been the prayer of Jesus and the Church (CCC 2585–2589). We pray them in the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours.
Teach that dryness and distractions are normal (CCC 2729–2733). Keep praying.
quiz: Vocal prayer uses…|Words|Dance|Silence only|Art|0|CCC 2700.
Meditation is…|Thinking with God|Daydreaming|Napping|Lecturing|0|CCC 2705.
Contemplation is…|Reading|Silent love of God|Counting|Singing|1|CCC 2709.
lessons.life: Try five minutes of lectio divina with a Gospel passage.
lessons.saint: John of the Cross: a poet and monk who showed how to rest in God.
misc: “Prayer is always asking for things.”
“If I am distracted, my prayer is worthless.”
lessons.mem: “O God, you are my God, I seek you, my soul thirsts for you.” (Psalm 63:1)
lessons.hook: Say “Wow,” “Please,” “For you,” “Thank you,” and “Hurray!” Ask which one is prayer. All five are.
lessons.assess: Ask children to name the five forms and give a short example of each.

script.open: Hand out a mock restaurant menu with five sections but no food names. Ask, “What would you order? Today we have a menu of ways to talk to God.”
teach: Say: “Prayer is the raising of the mind and heart to God. The Church teaches five forms of prayer. Blessing and adoration: we bless God and adore him as our Creator and Lord. Petition: we ask God for what we need, and for forgiveness. Intercession: we ask for others. Thanksgiving: we thank God for all he has given. Praise: we praise God just for who he is. For example, Psalm 63:1: ‘O God, you are my God, I seek you, my soul thirsts for you.’”

Say: “Prayer is also expressed in three ways. Vocal prayer uses words, aloud or silently, such as the Our Father or a prayer we make up. Meditation is thoughtful prayer: we think about a verse of the Bible or a scene from the Gospels, and ask, ‘What is God saying to me?’ Contemplation is a simple loving look at God. It is silent, resting in him, like looking at a friend without needing words. St. Teresa of Ávila called it ‘a close sharing between friends.’”

Say: “The Psalms are the prayer book of the Church. Every kind of prayer is in them: praise, thanks, sorrow, asking for help. Jesus prayed the Psalms. The Church prays them every day in the Liturgy of the Hours. A method of prayer called Lectio Divina means ‘divine reading’: read a short Scripture passage slowly, meditate on it, pray in response, and rest in silence. Prayer is a gift, and we learn it by praying.”
ask: Name the five forms of prayer. (Blessing/adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise.)
What are the three expressions? (Vocal, meditation, contemplation.)
What is Lectio Divina? (Prayerful reading of Scripture.)
practice: Give each child a “prayer menu” paper with five sections.
For each form of prayer, they write a short example: “Thank you for my family,” “Please help my friend who is sick,” “You are great, God.”
Try Lectio Divina together with Psalm 63:1-8: read it slowly twice, share one word, then keep silence for a minute.
Each child picks an item from the menu to pray this week.
script.close: Pray the Jesus Prayer slowly: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Choose a way of praying from your menu each day.”

tryit: Build a “prayer menu.”
Write an example for each of the five forms.
Try one.
lessons.saintStory:
Juan de Yepes was born in Spain in 1542, into a poor family. His father died when he was a little boy. He became a Carmelite friar, and took the name John of the Cross. He worked with Teresa of Ávila to reform the Carmelites.
Some of the friars didn’t like the reform. In 1577, they kidnapped John and locked him in a tiny cell in Toledo, where he was beaten and given little to eat. For nine months he lived in darkness. There, he composed some of the most beautiful poems in the Spanish language. He escaped one night by squeezing out of a window and climbing down a rope. He was weak, but he kept writing.
John of the Cross wrote about the “dark night,” when God seems far, and about resting in God’s love. He is a Doctor of the Church. He shows that prayer can also be silence, trust and waiting.

lessons.title: Liturgical year and the Mass
lessons.idea: The Church year unfolds the whole mystery of Christ, and the Mass is its center. The Mass has two main parts: the Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist. Jesus meets us in both, as on the road to Emmaus.
lessons.question: What is the structure of the Mass?
lessons.activity: “Mass map” (30 min). Fold a long strip into the parts of Mass: Introductory Rites, Liturgy of the Word, Liturgy of the Eucharist, Concluding Rites. Add details for each (Penitential Act, readings, homily, Creed, offertory, Eucharistic Prayer, Communion, blessing). Match to Emmaus. Rehearse the responses.
teach: The liturgical year celebrates the whole mystery of Christ (CCC 1163–1167). Sunday is the center, Easter is the feast of feasts (CCC 1168–1169).
The Mass has four parts: introductory rites, Liturgy of the Word, Liturgy of the Eucharist, concluding rites (CCC 1346–1355). The Emmaus story shows this shape (CCC 1347).
In the Eucharistic Prayer, the bread and wine become Christ’s Body and Blood (CCC 1375–1376). The Mass is the memorial and sacrifice of Calvary made present (CCC 1362–1367).
Encourage active participation: singing, responding and listening (CCC 1141).
talk: What is the structure of the Mass?
quiz: The Mass has…|Zero|One|Four main parts|Ten|2|CCC 1346.
The center of the liturgical year is…|Easter|Christmas|Lent|Ordinary Time|0|CCC 1169.
The Liturgy of the Word has…|Readings|Ads|Hymns only|Silence|0|CCC 1349.
lessons.life: Follow the readings in the missal at Mass.
lessons.saint: Stanislaus Kostka: a teenage student who loved the Eucharist and walked hundreds of miles to follow his calling.
misc: “The Mass is just a reminder of the Last Supper.”
“The priest does everything; we just watch.”
lessons.mem: “Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.” (Luke 24:29)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 24:13–35 in short pieces. Ask, “When did the disciples recognize Jesus?” (in the breaking of the bread). Ask which two parts of Mass match “scripture explained” and “bread broken.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to name the four parts of the Mass and one thing that happens in each.

script.open: Hand each child a long strip of paper. Say, “This is a path. We will walk it step by step, the way we walk through Mass. Every step is for something.”
teach: Say: “The Church’s year unfolds the whole story of Jesus. We have Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter, Pentecost and Ordinary Time. Each season lets us live a part of the mystery. And the heart of it all is the Mass. At Mass, Jesus is present, in his word and in the Eucharist. The Mass is the source and summit of our Christian life.”

Say: “The Mass has two main parts. First, the Liturgy of the Word. We gather and say sorry. We listen to readings from the Old Testament, a psalm, the New Testament and the Gospel. The priest gives a homily. We say the Creed and pray for the world. Second, the Liturgy of the Eucharist. The gifts of bread and wine are brought up. The priest says the Eucharistic Prayer. We pray the Our Father, share a sign of peace, and receive Communion. Then we are sent out: ‘Go in peace, glorifying the Lord by your life.’”

Read Luke 24:13-35 in summary. Say: “On the road to Emmaus, Jesus walked with two sad disciples. He explained the Scriptures, and their hearts burned. Then at supper, he broke the bread, and they recognized him. This is the shape of the Mass: Jesus speaks to us in the Word, and Jesus feeds us in the Eucharist. We meet him in both. Then, like the disciples, we go out to tell others.”
ask: What are the two main parts of the Mass? (The Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist.)
Where do we meet Jesus at Mass? (In his word and in the Eucharist.)
What happened on the road to Emmaus? (Jesus explained the Scriptures and broke bread.)
practice: Fold a long strip of paper into eight parts: Introductory Rites; First Reading; Psalm; Second Reading; Gospel and Homily; Eucharistic Prayer; Communion; Concluding Rites.
Write the name of each part on the front. On the back, write what happens, and draw a symbol.
Mark each part where Jesus meets us (the Word, the Eucharist).
Walk through the strip with a partner and explain it.
script.close: Pray the prayer: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Follow the parts of Mass next Sunday.”

tryit: Fold the strip into the parts of Mass.
Write what happens in each part.
Describe how Jesus meets us.
lessons.saintStory:
Stanislaus Kostka was born in Poland in 1550, to a noble family. At fourteen he went with his older brother to a school in Vienna. His brother was hard on him for being so serious about prayer and for attending Mass so often, and he often scolded him for it.
When he fell dangerously ill, he said that Mary came to him, with the child Jesus, and that he was healed. He wanted to join the Jesuits, but his father forbade it. So, at seventeen, Stanislaus slipped out of Vienna in disguise and walked hundreds of miles to Germany and then to Rome, where he was accepted by the Jesuit leader.
He lived as a novice for less than a year, praying and working with great joy. He died in 1568, at only seventeen. He is the patron of students. Stanislaus shows how much a young person can love Jesus in the Eucharist.

units.title: The Creed completed
units.eq: What else do we say when we say “I believe”?

lessons.title: Almighty Father: God’s power and care
lessons.idea: God is almighty because nothing is impossible for him, and his power is always used with love. He is Father to all he made and watches over everything he made, which is called providence.
lessons.question: What does it mean to call God almighty?
lessons.activity: Make two posters: “Things only God can do” and “How God uses his power to love.” Find one example of each in the Bible.
teach: God is almighty (CCC 268–274). “Nothing is impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). His power is shown most in mercy and forgiveness (CCC 270).
God is our Father and he cares for creation, which is called providence (CCC 302–305). He guides everything toward its goal without taking away our freedom.
Evil and suffering are real, and God does not cause evil. He is Father even when we cannot see it. Jesus trusted the Father even on the cross (CCC 306–314).
Teach with warmth. Some children have lost a parent or suffer at home. Say that God is close to all of them.
talk: How does a loving father use his strength?
When is it hard to trust that God cares?
quiz: “Almighty” means that…|God is far away|God is tired|God is angry|Nothing is impossible for God|3|CCC 268.
God’s providence means he…|Forgot about us|Is made of matter|Only watches|Cares for and guides all he made|3|CCC 302.
God shows his power most in…|Anger|Mercy and forgiveness|Punishing|Hiding|1|CCC 277.
lessons.life: Pray the Our Father slowly each night and thank God for one way he took care of you today.
lessons.saint: John Bosco: a priest who trusted God to provide for his boys.
misc: “Almighty means God does whatever he feels like.”
“If God is almighty, nothing bad could happen.”
lessons.mem: “With God all things are possible.” (Matthew 19:26)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If you could do anything, what would you do first?” Then say that God can do anything, and ask what he does with that power.
lessons.assess: Ask children to say what almighty means and one way God cares for them.

script.open: Show a picture of a very powerful thing (an avalanche or a rocket) and a picture of a mother holding a baby. Ask, “Which one shows more power? Which one shows more love? Is it possible to have both?” Say, “That is what we say about God.”
teach: Say: “The Creed begins, ‘I believe in God, the Father almighty.’ Almighty means that God can do anything. When Gabriel told Mary that Elizabeth was going to have a child, he said, ‘Nothing is impossible with God.’ (Luke 1:37) God made everything out of nothing. He controls nature. He raises the dead. But God never uses his power to hurt or to show off. His power is always used with love and with justice.”

Say: “God is our Father. A father cares for his children. Jesus said, ‘Do not be anxious about your life… Look at the birds of the air… your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?’ (Matthew 6:25-34) God knows each of us and loves us. He is Father of all things he has made. We can trust him.”

Say: “God watches over everything he has made. This is called providence. God guides the whole world toward its goal, and he cares for each person. Sometimes we do not understand why bad things happen. God allows evil in the world, because he gave us free will, and he can bring good out of it. But his love is never absent. We believe that his plan is good, and we pray, ‘Thy will be done.’”
ask: What does ‘almighty’ mean? (God can do anything.)
What is providence? (God’s loving care and guidance over everything.)
How is God’s power different from earthly power? (It is always used with love.)
practice: Make two posters. On the first: “Things only God can do” (create from nothing, forgive sins, raise the dead, know everything). On the second: “How God uses his power to love” (feeds the birds, healed the sick, saved us, calms the storm).
For each, find a Bible example (Genesis 1, Mark 2:5-12, John 11, Mark 4:35-41).
Add one example from your own life of God’s care.
Share posters in groups.
script.close: Pray the Our Father together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tell your family a time God took care of you.”

tryit: Make two posters.
“Things only God can do” and “How God uses his power to love.”
Find an example of each in the Bible.
lessons.saintStory:
John Bosco was born in 1815 in a poor farming family in northern Italy. His father died when he was two, and his mother, Margaret, raised him. As a boy he learned to do tricks like juggling and walking on a tightrope, to attract a crowd of friends, and then he would say the Rosary with them or repeat the sermon he had heard at Mass.
He became a priest and worked in the city of Turin, where many boys had no home or school. He gathered them in an “oratory,” and gave them food, lessons and prayer, but he had little money. Again and again, he trusted God to provide, and what he needed always seemed to come. He started schools and workshops, and a group of priests, the Salesians, to carry on the work.
Bosco died in 1888, having helped thousands of boys. He shows that God is almighty, and that his power is used with love.

lessons.title: He descended to the dead
lessons.idea: After Jesus died, his body lay in the tomb and his soul went to the place of the dead to free the holy people who waited for him. Holy Saturday is a day of quiet waiting before Easter.
lessons.question: What does it mean that Jesus descended to the dead?
lessons.activity: Mark Holy Saturday in a timeline from Good Friday to Easter. Draw the open doors of the tomb and the people who were waiting. Discuss why Saturday is quiet.
teach: Jesus really died. His body was in the tomb, and his soul went to the “abode of the dead,” called Sheol or Hades (CCC 632–633).
He did not go to the hell of the damned but to free the righteous who had died before him, from Adam on (CCC 633–634). An old Easter icon shows him taking Adam and Eve by the hands.
Holy Saturday is the Church’s quiet day. There is no Mass, and we wait at the tomb in hope (CCC 635–637).
Children may ask about people who died long ago. Explain that Christ’s saving work reaches all of history.
talk: Why do you think the Church is quiet on Holy Saturday?
What does it show that Jesus went to find those who had died?
How is waiting in hope different from waiting with fear?
quiz: Where did Jesus’ soul go after he died?|To the place of the damned|To the place of the dead to free the righteous|Straight to heaven|Nowhere|1|CCC 633.
What day do we keep as a day of quiet waiting?|Palm Sunday|Holy Saturday|Pentecost|Easter Monday|1|CCC 636.
An old Easter icon shows Jesus…|Pulling Adam and Eve from the tomb|Sleeping|Writing|Crying|0|Anastasis icon.
lessons.life: Take a few quiet minutes on Holy Saturday and pray for those who have died.
lessons.saint: Melito of Sardis: an early bishop who preached an Easter sermon about Christ’s victory.
misc: “Jesus went to hell to suffer.”
“Jesus’ soul left him for good.”
lessons.mem: “He descended into hell; on the third day he rose again from the dead.” (Apostles’ Creed)
lessons.hook: Light a candle and then cover it. Ask: “Is the light gone?” Wait. Then uncover it and say that the day between the Cross and Easter is like that.
lessons.assess: Ask children to tell what Jesus did between Friday and Sunday.

script.open: Hold a quiet moment: turn off the lights and say nothing for thirty seconds. Then whisper, “What was it like for the disciples on Saturday? Everything seemed to have ended. But something was happening that they could not see.”
teach: Read Matthew 27:57-66 in summary. Say: “Joseph of Arimathea laid Jesus’ body in his own tomb. A large stone was rolled across the door. The next day, which was the Sabbath, the chief priests and the Pharisees asked Pilate to put a guard on the tomb. That day, Holy Saturday, is the quietest day of the year. The Church does not celebrate Mass. The altar is bare. We wait.”

Say: “The Apostles’ Creed says, ‘He descended into hell’ or ‘He descended to the dead.’ It does not mean the hell of the damned. It means the place of the dead, sometimes called Sheol or Hades. Jesus really died: his soul separated from his body. His body lay in the tomb. His soul went to the place of the dead, where the holy ones waited, Adam and Eve, Abraham, Moses, David, and all those who had lived faithfully before Christ. 1 Peter 3:18-20 says that Christ ‘went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison.’”

Say: “There he announced the good news and opened the gates of heaven to the just. In icons of the Resurrection in the Eastern Church, Jesus is shown pulling Adam and Eve out of their graves. This is a picture of what he did. Jesus’ death is a victory, not a defeat. Holy Saturday teaches us to wait in hope, trusting that something is happening in the silence.”
ask: What does ‘He descended to the dead’ mean? (Jesus’ soul went to the place of the dead to free the holy ones.)
Who did Jesus free? (Adam and Eve and all the just who waited.)
What is Holy Saturday like in the Church? (Quiet, no Mass, waiting.)
practice: Draw a timeline from Good Friday to Easter, with three parts: Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
On Saturday, draw the tomb with the doors open, and Jesus reaching out to Adam, Eve and the holy people.
Write a caption: “Jesus set the just free.”
Share and talk about waiting in hope.
script.close: Pray quietly: “Jesus, we wait in hope.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Spend a few minutes in quiet on Holy Saturday.”

tryit: Mark Holy Saturday on the timeline.
Draw the open doors of the tomb.
Draw the people who waited.
lessons.saintStory:
Melito was bishop of Sardis, a city in what is now Turkey, around the year 170. We know little about his life, but he was highly respected, and traveled to the Holy Land to learn about the books of the Old Testament. He wrote a number of works.
One of them survives, a homily on Easter, called On Pascha. Melito describes how Jesus, the Lamb, was sacrificed for us, and how, in his death, he conquered death. He says that Christ is the one who “rescued us from slavery to freedom, from darkness to light, from death to life.” The early Church loved this idea: when Jesus died, his soul descended to the place of the dead, and he set the just free.
Melito reminds us of how ancient our faith is. The words “He descended to the dead” belong to the Creed, and they tell us what Jesus did on Holy Saturday.

lessons.title: Amen: our yes to God
lessons.idea: “Amen” means “so be it” and “I believe it.” We say it at the end of the Creed and our prayers to say yes to God. The Creed ends with the hope of life everlasting.
lessons.question: Why do we say Amen?
lessons.activity: Say a prayer together and put in a loud, joyful Amen. Draw a banner with the word AMEN and a prayer you will say it to.
teach: “Amen” is a Hebrew word for “so be it” and “it is true” (CCC 1061–1065). It is the last word of the Bible (Revelation 22:21) and of the Creed.
Jesus is called “the Amen,” the faithful witness (Revelation 3:14). All God’s promises find their “Yes” in him (2 Corinthians 1:20).
We say Amen at Communion when we say yes to Jesus. It means “I believe it is you.”
Teach children to say it clearly and with meaning.
talk: When do we say Amen at Mass?
Why is it good to say it out loud?
What would you like to say Amen to?
quiz: “Amen” means…|Maybe|So be it, I believe|Stop|Goodbye|1|CCC 1061.
At Communion we say Amen to…|The song|The end|The sermon|Jesus in the Eucharist|3|CCC 1396.
Who is called “the Amen”?|Peter|Moses|Noah|Jesus|3|Revelation 3:14.
lessons.life: Say Amen carefully at every prayer this week, and notice what you are saying yes to.
lessons.saint: Joseph: the quiet man whose whole life was a yes to God.
misc: “Amen is just a way to end a prayer.”
“It only means the end.”
lessons.mem: “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why we utter the Amen through him.” (2 Corinthians 1:20)
lessons.hook: Ask a question with a clear answer, such as “Is Jesus risen?” and have the class answer together. Say that this kind of answer is an Amen.
lessons.assess: Ask children to explain what Amen means and use it in a prayer.

script.open: Say a series of statements, some true and some false. After each one, the children respond, “Amen!” if it is true. For example: “God is good.” “God made the world.” “The sky is made of cheese.” Say, “‘Amen’ means ‘so be it, I agree.’ Today we will see why it matters.”
teach: Say: “‘Amen’ is a Hebrew word that means ‘so be it,’ ‘it is true,’ and ‘I believe it.’ We say it at the end of the Creed and at the end of nearly every prayer. We say it when we receive Communion: the priest says, ‘The Body of Christ,’ and we say, ‘Amen.’ We are saying, ‘Yes, I believe this is Jesus.’”

Read Revelation 3:14 and 2 Corinthians 1:20. Say: “Jesus is called ‘the Amen, the faithful and true witness.’ In him, all of God’s promises are ‘Yes.’ When we say ‘Amen’ to God, we say yes to what he has said, to what he has promised and to what he asks of us. Mary’s ‘let it be done to me’ was an Amen. Joseph’s obedience was an Amen.”

Say: “The Creed ends with the words ‘life everlasting. Amen.’ This is our hope: that we will live with God forever. We pray with confidence. We say Amen aloud, not as a mumble. It is a sign that we mean what we say, and that we belong to the Church’s prayer. And when we say it with our lives, by trusting God and doing what he asks, we are saying Amen with our whole selves.”
ask: What does ‘Amen’ mean? (So be it, I believe.)
When do we say Amen? (End of prayers, the Creed, at Communion.)
How can we say Amen with our lives? (By trusting God and doing what he asks.)
practice: Say a short prayer together, for example the Glory Be, and shout a loud, joyful “Amen!”
Give each child a paper strip to make a banner with the word AMEN in large decorated letters.
Under it, write a prayer you will say every day this week (Our Father, Hail Mary, Creed).
Hang the banners in a row.
script.close: Pray the Creed together, ending with a strong “Amen!” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say Amen with meaning at Mass.”

tryit: Say a prayer with a loud Amen.
Make an AMEN banner.
Choose a prayer to say every day.
lessons.saintStory:
Joseph is the quietest person in the Gospels. Not one word he said is recorded. But everything he did was a yes to God.
When Joseph found that Mary was expecting a child, he was going to quietly step aside. Then an angel told him in a dream, “Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife.” Joseph got up and did what the angel said. Later, in other dreams, he was told to take the child to Egypt, and then to return to Nazareth. Each time, he obeyed right away. He worked as a carpenter to support his family.
Joseph is the patron of the Universal Church, of fathers, and of workers. His life is like a long “Amen.” He shows that saying yes to God, quietly and faithfully, is the greatest thing we can do.
